abstract: ArXiv:2609.19642v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Peptide-HLA binding prediction is a critical step in neoantigen identification for personalized cancer immunotherapy and holds significant clinical value. However, the training data available for many HLA alleles are extremely limited, which severely constrains the performance of conventional methods on this task. Parameterized quantum circuits are hypothesized to induce inductive biases beneficial for learning from small datasets, yet their application to biological sequence prediction remains underexplored. To address this, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical neural network (HQNN) specifically designed for peptide-HLA binding prediction. HQNN integrates multi-source biological feature encoding with parallel quantum feature extractors and a quantum-enhanced classifier. On two HLA alleles (A*02:01 and B*07:02), HQNN outperforms a parameter-matched classical CNN baseline across all training sizes, with the performance gap widening as training data decreases. Ablation studies confirm the respective contributions of the quantum feature extraction module and the quantum classifier. In noise-aware simulations, performance degrades only mildly, and such degradation is reasonable and acceptable under realistic quantum hardware noise levels. These results suggest that hybrid quantum-classical architectures can provide practical sample-efficiency gains for immunoinformatics tasks in low-data regimes.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical neural network is proposed for peptide-HLA binding prediction, showing sample-efficiency gains over a parameter-matched classical CNN in low-data regimes.
motivation: Training data for many HLA alleles is extremely scarce, limiting conventional predictors, and parameterized quantum circuits are hypothesized to provide inductive biases useful for small datasets, yet their use in biological sequence prediction is underexplored.
method: The authors build a hybrid quantum-classical model combining multi-source biological feature encoding, parallel quantum feature extractors, and a quantum-enhanced classifier, evaluated against a parameter-matched classical CNN with ablation and noise-aware simulations.
result: On HLA alleles A*02:01 and B*07:02 the model outperforms the classical baseline at all training sizes, with the gap widening as data decreases, and performance degrades only mildly under realistic hardware noise.
conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical architectures may offer practical sample-efficiency benefits for immunoinformatics tasks, though the work is applied machine learning rather than an information-theoretic advance.

title: Polynomially Larger Deletion Codes By Linear Hashing Of Substring Counts
authors: Eyal En Gad
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19493v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that binary codes of length [MATH] correcting two deletions exist with redundancy [MATH]. The previous best upper bound had leading coefficient [MATH], unchanged since 1965, while the best known lower bound has coefficient [MATH]. More generally, codes correcting [MATH] deletions exist with redundancy [MATH], improving the coefficient [MATH]. We extract a code from one label class of a random linear hash of substring counts, with about [MATH] times fewer labels than a direct construction. Confusable words that still share a label are separated by a two-colouring after discarding the words in components with odd cycles, and these are few because an odd cycle forces the edits along it to overlap.
tldr: The paper constructs classical binary deletion-correcting codes with improved redundancy scaling by extracting a code from one label class of a random linear hash of substring counts.
motivation: Deletion-correcting codes are central to DNA data storage and synchronization, but the leading coefficient in the redundancy of codes correcting multiple deletions has stagnated since 1965.
method: A random linear hash of substring counts is used to define labels; one label class is selected with substantially fewer labels than a direct construction, and residual confusable words are separated by two-colouring after discarding components with odd cycles, which are rare because odd cycles force overlapping edits.
result: Binary codes of length n correcting two deletions are shown to exist with redundancy 4 log n + o(log n) (coefficient reduced from the previous best 15), and more generally codes correcting k deletions achieve redundancy 4k log n, improving the coefficient over prior bounds.
conclusion: The linear-hashing viewpoint yields polynomially larger deletion codes and improves a long-standing upper bound, though the contribution is confined to classical coding theory.

title: Suzuki-Trotter Decompositions And Other Methods For Quantum Time Evolution
authors: Johann Ostmeyer
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19184v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: (Suzuki-)Trotter decompositions, splitting methods, (Lie) product formulae... The most common numerical methods for the time evolution of quantum systems come with many names. And they are used practically everywhere with applications ranging from the solution of classical equations of motion and various Monte Carlo simulations to the real and imaginary time evolution on classical as well as quantum computers. Here we review the state of the art of said methods, focussing especially on the progress made over the last few years. We highlight recently discovered efficient time evolution algorithms and explain how best to use them in practice. A central part of this work is the estimation of error bounds that has improved greatly within the past decade. The relevance of time evolution methods for quantum computing is discussed with a focus on noisy hardware. Finally, a comprehensive overview of generalisations, related methods and alternatives to Trotterization is provided. This includes time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics, processed methods, multi-product formulae, symplectic integrators, TDVP for tensor networks, quantum signal processing, Crouch-Grossman methods and more. The overall perspective in this work is that of a theoretical physicist. All mathematical proofs as well as some technical details are omitted for easier readability. Instead, this review serves as a hands-on guide and, of course, as a starting point for references that provide further details.
tldr: A review of Suzuki-Trotter decompositions and related numerical methods for quantum time evolution, covering error bounds, practical algorithms, and extensions for quantum computing.
motivation: Time evolution methods are ubiquitous in quantum simulation and classical/quantum computation, but their error bounds and practical implementation have improved significantly in recent years, motivating a comprehensive guide.
method: The paper reviews splitting methods, product formulae, error estimates, and alternatives such as TDVP, quantum signal processing, and symplectic integrators, with a focus on noisy quantum hardware.
result: It provides a state-of-the-art overview of efficient time evolution algorithms, improved error bounds, and a hands-on guide to selecting and applying these methods.
conclusion: The review serves as a practical starting point for researchers needing time evolution methods, though it omits detailed proofs and technical derivations.

title: AlchemQ: Proof-Carrying Quantum Circuit Optimization With Per-Result Equivalence Certificates
authors: Adam Laabs
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present AlchemQ v0.5, a proof-of-concept system that couples an untrusted beam-search optimizer with a machine-checkable per-result certification layer and a versioned certificate protocol (0.2.0), so that every optimized circuit ships with a verifiable artifact rather than a bare claim. The certifier proves equivalence up to global phase by ZX-calculus full reduction, with a numeric-tensor fallback based on the optimal Hilbert-Schmidt overlap. Certificates are self-contained and tamper-evident: canonical gate-canon-v1 hashes, measured residuals, tri-state verdicts (certified/rejected/inconclusive), and versioned phase-note schemas for cross-platform reproducibility. The agent aggregates three fuzzy t-norms, cannot return an uncertified circuit, and since v0.4 guarantees no componentwise regression against the original. On a benchmark of 100 circuits, all 400 optimizations terminate without error, every returned circuit is certified, every mutation is detected, and a 2998-test suite passes on two platforms. The PyZX baseline is strong (21.4% mean T-count reduction over 82 circuits) and the agent is strictly better on 9/100; the three t-norms return identical circuits on all 100 standard instances, diverging only on 4/38 of an adversarial suite. Two case studies are new: a false negative root-caused to a pivot-normalization bug in PyZX's compare_tensors (pivot 4.7e-9; the optimal-overlap residual is 7.4e-11), and eight certificates rejected on macOS due to BLAS-dependent floats in phase_note. Both were fixed; all artifact sets validate 400/400 on both platforms. A pilot run on IBM Heron r2 gives a certified circuit 78% shallower with 65% fewer two-qubit gates; output quality favors it on all three metrics but is not significant at 1024 shots. We release the certificate specification and a standalone reference verifier (Apache-2.0) with data and scripts; the engine is proprietary.
tldr: AlchemQ is a proof-carrying quantum circuit optimizer that produces per-result equivalence certificates using ZX-calculus and numeric overlap checks.
motivation: Quantum circuit optimizers may return incorrect or unverifiable results, so machine-checkable certificates are needed to guarantee equivalence up to global phase.
method: It couples an untrusted beam-search optimizer with a certifier that performs ZX-calculus full reduction, a tensor-based fallback using optimal Hilbert-Schmidt overlap, canonical gate hashes, and versioned certificate schemas.
result: On 100 benchmark circuits and 400 optimizations, all returned circuits were certified, mutations were detected, a 2998-test suite passed on two platforms, and an IBM Heron r2 pilot produced 78% shallower circuits with 65% fewer two-qubit gates but without statistical significance at 1024 shots.
conclusion: The system provides tamper-evident, reproducible certificates for quantum circuit optimization, with a released specification and reference verifier, though the optimization engine remains proprietary.

title: Quantum Computers Will Not Be That Different: A Blueprint For Quantum Computer Architecture At Scale
authors: Matthias Troyer Torsten Hoefler
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computers are technologically novel and unusual, but at system scale they should be engineered using many of the same principles that govern classical heterogeneous accelerators. This paper argues that utility-scale quantum architecture is primarily a cost-performance problem across a coupled quantum-classical system, leading to a blueprint for scalable quantum processing unit (QPU) design. Our architecture blueprint is organized around clean logical abstractions, hiding details and complexity of physical qubit modalities below the instruction set architecture (ISA) boundary, and specializes recurring functions aggressively to minimize the cost for utility scale quantum computations. Its low-level implementation through specialized local hardware for control, readout, and quantum error correction (QEC) closely resembles the architecture of high-performance network stacks. One of our main insights is that the design principles and the resulting architecture closely follow established practice from classical computing and networking.
tldr: The paper argues that utility-scale quantum computers should be engineered like classical heterogeneous accelerators, proposing a blueprint for scalable QPU architecture organized around clean logical abstractions and specialized local hardware for control, readout, and QEC.
motivation: As quantum computers scale, their design becomes primarily a cost-performance problem across a coupled quantum-classical system, requiring system-level engineering principles analogous to classical computing and networking.
method: The authors propose an architectural blueprint that hides physical qubit modality details below an ISA boundary, specializes recurring functions aggressively, and implements low-level control, readout, and QEC via specialized local hardware resembling high-performance network stacks.
result: The blueprint yields a scalable QPU design that mirrors established practice from classical computing and networking, emphasizing abstraction, specialization, and tight integration of quantum and classical components.
conclusion: Quantum computer architecture at scale will likely converge on principles from classical heterogeneous computing and networking, making quantum computers not fundamentally different as systems.

title: Surjective Fischer--Musz\'ely Maps On Positive Cones Of JB-algebras
authors: Shiho Oi Osamu Hatori
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19668v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that every surjective Fischer--Musz\'ely map between positive cones of arbitrary JB-algebras is additive and positively homogeneous, and extends uniquely to a bounded positive linear surjection. In particular, this gives a complete affirmative answer to Moln\'ar's problem for arbitrary [MATH]-algebras. The theorem includes nonunital and exceptional JB-algebras and assumes neither injectivity nor continuity. The proof connects the norm-valued functional equation to positive-cone rigidity through translation invariance of an induced pseudometric. For a surjective map satisfying the Fischer--Musz\'ely identity with uniform error [MATH], we also construct a unique bounded positive linear map [MATH] at uniform distance at most [MATH]. The set [MATH] is dense in [MATH], although [MATH] need not be surjective, even when the original map is continuous and bijective. For bijective FM maps, we obtain weighted Jordan representations on the biduals. We also extend the characterization of surjective norm-sum preservers to JB-algebras and characterize norm arithmetic-midpoint and harmonic-mean identities on positive invertible cones of unital JB-algebras.
tldr: The paper proves that surjective Fischer--Muszély maps between positive cones of JB-algebras are additive and positively homogeneous, extending to bounded positive linear surjections, and resolves Molnár's problem for arbitrary JB-algebras.
motivation: The Fischer--Muszély identity and preserver problems on operator algebras are fundamental structural questions, with Molnár's problem asking whether surjective maps preserving this identity must be linear.
method: The proof connects a norm-valued functional equation to positive-cone rigidity via translation invariance of an induced pseudometric, and also constructs bounded positive linear maps at uniform distance for approximately FM maps.
result: Surjective FM maps on positive cones of arbitrary JB-algebras are additive, positively homogeneous, and extend uniquely to bounded positive linear surjections; weighted Jordan representations and characterizations of norm-sum preservers are obtained.
conclusion: The work fully answers Molnár's problem for JB-algebras without injectivity or continuity assumptions, extending known results to nonunital and exceptional cases.

title: Collective Symmetry And Criticality From Single-Component Fluctuations
authors: Chunhao Guo, Zhe Wang, Zheng Yan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19629v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Symmetry plays a fundamental role in modern physics by guiding the classification of phases and the construction of effective theories of critical systems. Identifying collective symmetry remains challenging because tests based on preselected order parameters can overlook hidden components. A central goal is therefore to extract symmetry and critical information from a single accessible component. We pursue this goal using Lee--Yang zero ratios generated by a single ordering field. Unmeasured components shape the projected fluctuation distribution and hence the relative zero positions. Deep in a phase with spontaneous symmetry breaking, we show analytically that the zero ratios for an isotropic order parameter approach a parameter-free Bessel sequence fixed by the number of collective components. Near quantum criticality, fluctuations deform this distribution. The resulting ratio deviations and their finite-size coupling dependence carry additional critical information. We demonstrate these results with large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations of many-body systems with conventional and enlarged continuous symmetries. This approach provides quantitative access to collective symmetry and criticality without measuring every competing order.
tldr: The paper uses Lee-Yang zero ratios from a single ordering field to extract collective symmetry and critical information in many-body systems, demonstrated via quantum Monte Carlo simulations.
motivation: Identifying collective symmetries and critical properties is challenging because tests based on preselected order parameters can miss hidden components, so the authors aim to access symmetry and criticality from a single measurable component.
method: They analytically study Lee-Yang zero ratios generated by a single ordering field for isotropic order parameters deep in a symmetry-broken phase and near quantum criticality, and perform large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations of systems with conventional and enlarged continuous symmetries.
result: Deep in the symmetry-broken phase, the zero ratios approach a parameter-free Bessel sequence determined by the number of collective components; near criticality, fluctuations deform this distribution, and the ratio deviations and finite-size coupling dependence encode additional critical information.
conclusion: This approach provides quantitative access to collective symmetry and criticality without measuring every competing order, offering a new probe for many-body quantum systems.

title: Unitary TQFTs, Unitary Disk-like $n$-categories, And Higher Hilbert Spaces
authors: Greyson Wesley
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the notion of a unitary disk-like [MATH]-category, which is a disk-like [MATH]-category equipped with a reflection structure and a sphere trace inducing positive-definite pairings. Since a finite unitary disk-like [MATH]-category is defined to be the local field data of a fully extended [MATH]D unitary TQFT, we propose a complete finite unitary disk-like [MATH]-category as the definition of a finite [MATH]-Hilbert space for all [MATH]. For [MATH] and [MATH] we verify this proposal, proving that complete finite unitary disk-like 1- and 2-categories are isometrically equivalent to finite 2- and 3-Hilbert spaces respectively, and that these equivalences are functorial. For [MATH] we recover a unitary refinement of Schommer-Pries' classification of oriented [MATH]D TQFTs in terms of [MATH]-Morita equivalence classes of [MATH]-algebras, and for [MATH] we categorify this to classify oriented [MATH]D unitary TQFTs by [MATH]-Morita equivalence classes of [MATH]-multifusion categories. Along the way, we investigate fully incomplete 3-Hilbert spaces, prove a strictification result for pivotal dagger 2-categories, and define functors and higher transformations between disk-like [MATH]-categories.
tldr: The paper proposes a definition of finite n-Hilbert spaces using complete finite unitary disk-like n-categories and classifies unitary TQFTs via higher Morita equivalence.
motivation: To provide a higher-categorical foundation for unitary topological quantum field theory and to generalize finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces to higher categories.
method: Introduces unitary disk-like n-categories with reflection structure and positive-definite sphere trace, proves equivalences to finite n-Hilbert spaces for n=1,2, and recovers/categorifies classification results for oriented TQFTs.
result: Complete finite unitary disk-like 1- and 2-categories are functorially isometrically equivalent to finite 2- and 3-Hilbert spaces; oriented 2D and 3D unitary TQFTs are classified by Morita equivalence classes of algebras and multifusion categories.
conclusion: The work establishes a higher-categorical framework for unitary TQFTs and higher Hilbert spaces, with potential applications to mathematical physics but not directly to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Equivalence Between Nested Gibbs Measures And Log-Linear Combinations Of Gibbs Measures
authors: Yaiza Bermudez, Samir M. Perlaza, I\~naki Esnaola
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19988v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, three operations on Gibbs probability measures are studied. The first operation, often referred to as renormalization, takes one Gibbs probability measure and generates a new Gibbs measure by normalizing a power of its density. This normalization has a twofold effect: it changes the regularization factor and concentrates the support within a subset of the original support. Interestingly, these effects can be independently controlled by different parameters. The second operation consists of a normalized log-linear combination of the densities of Gibbs probability measures. The third operation takes two Gibbs probability measures and changes the reference measure of the latter with the former. Hence, the former is said to be "nested" within the latter, yielding a new Gibbs probability measure. The resulting measures from the second and third operations are also Gibbs probability measures and are shown, respectively, to solve optimization problems involving the expectations of linear combinations of the objective functions of the given measures, subject to a relative entropy regularization. These optimization problems differ exclusively in the coefficients of the linear combinations. This leads to the conclusion that there exists a set of parameters for which nesting one Gibbs probability measure into another has the same effect as log-linearly combining them. These operations have relevant applications in statistical learning. As an example, a one-shot federated learning system in which clients send their locally trained Gibbs algorithms to the server for log-linear combination is shown to achieve the same performance as a Gibbs algorithm trained upon the aggregation of all local training datasets.
tldr: The paper proves an equivalence between nesting Gibbs probability measures and log-linear combinations of Gibbs measures, with applications to statistical learning and federated learning.
motivation: To clarify how different operations on Gibbs measures relate to each other and to optimization problems with relative entropy regularization.
method: Three operations on Gibbs measures are studied: renormalization, normalized log-linear combination, and nesting; their optimization interpretations and equivalence conditions are derived.
result: The operations produce Gibbs measures, and for certain parameters nesting is equivalent to log-linear combination; a one-shot federated learning system using log-linear aggregation matches the performance of a centrally trained Gibbs algorithm.
conclusion: The equivalence provides a unified theoretical basis for Gibbs measure operations and supports log-linear aggregation in federated learning.

title: Vehicle-Routing Clustering By Sparse Quantum Relaxation
authors: Bilal Farooq Farzan Moosavi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19575v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the cluster-assignment layer of a cluster-first-route-second decomposition for the capacitated pickup-and-delivery problem with time windows (CPDPTW), instead of a direct route-ordering quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO). Sample-based subspace diagonalization (SQD) degenerates to best-of-shots for any diagonal optimization Hamiltonian, so a useful transfer to routing requires non-diagonal relaxation. Quantum random access optimization (QRAO) provides this non-diagonality by encoding binary variables through non-commuting quantum random access code (QRAC) observables. CPDPTW-derived conflict graphs expose a routing-specific obstruction because dense objectives and penalty-encoded constraints destroy QRAO compression. We keep the Hamiltonian sparse by encoding only the sparsified objective and enforcing one-hot, capacity, and cluster time-budget feasibility by repair after rounding. We make no quantum-advantage claim. Under strong repair the classical pass alone reaches near-optimal cost at the tested sizes. The result is a regime map linking sparsification, achieved compression, linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) 1-norm, heavy-hex two-qubit depth, sampling drift, and final routing quality on Qiskit Aer, calibrated FakeTorino, and IBM Heron ibm_quebec. Across a 108-row ideal-calibrated-hardware evaluation grid spanning four to twelve pickup-delivery request pairs, the hardware slice has mean gap 0.0016 and mean device-vs-ideal total variation distance (TVD) 0.279; a decoder ablation at sizes six through twelve isolates the non-diagonal signal.
tldr: This paper develops a sparse quantum relaxation approach for the cluster-assignment layer of a capacitated pickup-and-delivery routing problem, using QRAO and QRAC observables on IBM quantum hardware.
motivation: Direct QUBO formulations for routing are limited by dense Hamiltonians and penalty constraints, so the authors seek a non-diagonal quantum relaxation that can handle routing-specific conflict graphs and preserve sparsity.
method: They encode only the sparsified objective into a QRAO Hamiltonian, enforce feasibility via classical repair after rounding, and evaluate across a 108-row grid on Qiskit Aer, calibrated FakeTorino, and IBM Heron ibm_quebec, including a decoder ablation.
result: The hardware slice achieves mean gap 0.0016 and mean device-vs-ideal TVD 0.279, while under strong repair the classical pass alone reaches near-optimal cost at tested sizes.
conclusion: The work provides a regime map linking sparsification, compression, LCU 1-norm, heavy-hex depth, sampling drift, and routing quality, but makes no quantum-advantage claim.

title: Sum Of Self-commutators Of Commuting Operators
authors: Sameer Chavan, Md. Ramiz Reza, Shanola S. Sequeira
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It is well known that every hyponormal operator on a complex Hilbert space whose spectrum has planar Lebesgue measure zero is normal. In particular, every compact hyponormal operator on a complex Hilbert space is normal. In this paper, we investigate analogous structural and spectral phenomena for so-called sum-hyponormal [MATH]-tuples on a complex Hilbert space [MATH], namely, commuting [MATH]-tuples [MATH] satisfying [MATH]. We show that every sum-hyponormal [MATH]-tuple of compact operators decomposes as the direct sum of a normal [MATH]-tuple and a quasinilpotent sum-hyponormal [MATH]-tuple. As a consequence, every sum-hyponormal [MATH]-tuple on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space is normal. In contrast to the single-operator case, a sum-hyponormal [MATH]-tuple need not be normaloid. Nevertheless, we establish a multivariable analogue of Putnam's inequality for sum-hyponormal [MATH]-tuples with commuting imaginary parts. As a consequence, we prove that [MATH] is normal whenever the planar Lebesgue measure of [MATH] is zero, where [MATH] denotes the Taylor spectrum of [MATH] and [MATH] is the complex-linear polynomial with alternating coefficients [MATH] and [MATH].
tldr: The paper extends classical structural and spectral results for hyponormal operators to sum-hyponormal commuting n-tuples on Hilbert space, deriving a decomposition theorem and a multivariable Putnam inequality.
motivation: Motivated by the known fact that compact hyponormal operators are normal, the authors seek analogous phenomena for commuting tuples satisfying a sum-of-self-commutators condition.
method: Pure operator-theoretic and multivariable spectral analysis, using the Taylor spectrum of commuting tuples and a multivariable analogue of Putnam's inequality under the assumption of commuting imaginary parts.
result: Every sum-hyponormal tuple of compact operators decomposes as a normal tuple direct-sum a quasinilpotent sum-hyponormal tuple, so finite-dimensional sum-hyponormal tuples are normal, and normality follows when the planar measure of the polynomial image of the Taylor spectrum vanishes.
conclusion: The results show both parallels and contrasts with the single-operator theory—e.g., sum-hyponormal tuples need not be normaloid—clarifying the structure of this class of multi-operator tuples.

title: Qupertino: Pure Mlx Array Kernels Versus Hand-Tuned Metal Shaders For Quantum Circuit Simulation On Apple Silicon
authors: Shlomo Kashani
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present Qupertino, an open-source quantum circuit simulator for Apple Silicon, and use it to ask how far a simulator written purely in MLX array operations can go and what remains for hand-tuned Metal shaders. The framework ships two measured tiers. The pure tier dispatches structured gates to specialized MLX kernels: diagonal gates run as broadcast phase multiplies, controlled gates as masked half-state updates, and SWAP as an axis permutation; a paired dense-path ablation attributes a 25-33x speedup to this dispatch alone. The opt-in shader tier adds hand-written Metal kernels for every structured layer family in our benchmarks, including phase-LUT diagonals, GF(2) affine permutation gathers, fused tensor-product single-qubit layers, radix-4 QFT and Walsh-Hadamard butterflies, and basis-conjugated XX/YY Trotter layers; runtime fusion detectors route work to them while preserving circuit semantics exactly, confirmed by parity tests. In a four-way interleaved campaign on M1 Max (two warmups, ten measured repeats per cell), the shader tier is fastest by mean runtime in all 18 comparison cells against same-machine Qiskit Aer CPU and PennyLane lightning.qubit. At 25 qubits, gate-stream QFT runs in 0.0591 +/- 0.0029 s (paired 47.2x over Aer, 95.3x over PennyLane) and TFIM Trotter evolution in 0.495 +/- 0.035 s (36.2x and 67.2x). Across a 29-workload suite, the shader tier's paired speedup over pure MLX reaches 25x, with 25 of 29 workloads accelerating above parity. The framework also supports variational ansatz workloads, QAOA, QCBM, Trotter-Suzuki Hamiltonian simulation, and OpenQASM 2.0 import (unitary subset); a preliminary MPS backend reaches 150 qubits on limited-entanglement workloads. Correctness rests on 253 Python tests, independent complex128 checks, and a Trotter-error curve against exact diagonalization. State-vector memory remains exponential in qubit count.
tldr: Qupertino is an open-source quantum circuit simulator for Apple Silicon that compares pure MLX array operations with hand-tuned Metal shaders.
motivation: To explore how far pure array-based simulation can go and what performance gains hand-tuned GPU shaders provide for quantum circuit simulation on Apple hardware.
method: Implements a pure MLX tier with specialized kernels for structured gates and an opt-in Metal shader tier with fused kernels, then benchmarks against Qiskit Aer and PennyLane lightning.qubit.
result: Shader tier achieves up to 47.2x speedup over Aer and 95.3x over PennyLane for QFT, and 25x over pure MLX across 29 workloads.
conclusion: Hand-tuned Metal shaders substantially outperform pure MLX array operations, but state-vector memory remains exponential; the framework supports variational and Trotter workloads.

title: Three-Dimensional Coulomb Discrete Spectrum Via Symplectic Geometry And Phase-Space Constraints: A Geometric Framework For Condensed-Matter Coulomb-Like Systems
authors: Gang Zheng, Peng Chen, Mengli Wang, Wenqi Xue, Benniu Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19159v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discrete energy-level structures in Coulomb-like localized bound states are conventionally obtained by direct diagonalization of the Schr\"odinger equation or by semiclassical approximations that fail at low energies. Here we develop a geometric phase-space framework that recovers the exact discrete energy levels and shell degeneracy of three-dimensional Coulomb bound states from classical symplectic geometry and global boundary constraints, bypassing explicit operator diagonalization. Using Kustaanheimo--Stiefel regularization, we map negative-energy Kepler orbits to four-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillators. The group composition law of the symplectic flow determines an integral kernel built from the classical two-point action and Van Vleck amplitude, whose infinitesimal generator satisfies an exact linear evolution equation---a property we term . Imposing three geometric constraints---decay at infinity, regularity at the origin, and fiber invariance under the Hopf fibration---we recover the exact [MATH] scaling and [MATH] degeneracy. The phase scale [MATH] sets the action unit; all spectral structural features are independent of its value. This framework offers a symmetry-transparent route to spectral data: for quadratic Hamiltonians, the classical kernel incurs zero semiclassical error even at ground-state energies, and the geometric constraints directly identify symmetry-protected degeneracies without diagonalization. We apply the method to shallow impurity states, moir\'e superlattices, and semiclassical transport, demonstrating how geometric screening rules simplify spectral analysis in condensed-matter environments.
tldr: A geometric phase-space framework using symplectic geometry and Kustaanheimo–Stiefel regularization recovers the exact discrete spectrum and degeneracy of three-dimensional Coulomb bound states without operator diagonalization.
motivation: Conventional methods for obtaining Coulomb bound-state spectra rely on direct diagonalization or semiclassical approximations that fail at low energies, motivating a symmetry-transparent geometric approach.
method: The authors map negative-energy Kepler orbits to four-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillators via Kustaanheimo–Stiefel regularization, construct an integral kernel from the classical two-point action and Van Vleck amplitude, and impose geometric constraints from decay, regularity, and Hopf fibration invariance.
result: The framework recovers the exact inverse-square energy scaling and quadratic degeneracy of 3D Coulomb bound states, with zero semiclassical error for quadratic Hamiltonians, independent of the phase scale.
conclusion: This provides a geometric route to spectral data and is applied to shallow impurity states, moiré superlattices, and semiclassical transport in condensed-matter environments.

title: Time-resolved Topology Of Aperiodically Driven Systems
authors: Justin T. Cole, Christina J\"org, Terry A. Loring, Alexander Cerjan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological phases of periodically driven systems are commonly classified through Floquet Hamiltonians, whose definition relies on a repeated driving cycle. However, this framework breaks down for systems whose realized evolution is aperiodic or nonlinear, even when robust topological phenomena appear to persist. Here, we introduce an evolution-history spectral localizer framework that classifies Chern topology directly from a system's finite-time unitary evolution operator. The method produces a time-resolved local Chern marker and an associated local gap, allowing topology and its protection to be tracked during the actual dynamics of a driven system. We demonstrate this approach in quasiperiodically driven and nonlinear photonic models, where it identifies transient topological protection, its subsequent loss, and the recovery of topology after nonlinear excitations disperse. The developed framework provides a route for analyzing driven photonic systems whose topological behavior depends on finite-time dynamics rather than an idealized Floquet cycle.
tldr: The paper introduces an evolution-history spectral localizer framework to classify Chern topology directly from finite-time unitary evolution operators in aperiodically driven systems.
motivation: Floquet Hamiltonians fail to describe aperiodic or nonlinear driven systems even when robust topological phenomena persist, motivating a time-resolved topological classification.
method: The authors develop a spectral localizer based on the evolution history that yields a time-resolved local Chern marker and associated local gap, tracking topology and protection during actual dynamics.
result: Applied to quasiperiodically driven and nonlinear photonic models, the method identifies transient topological protection, its loss, and recovery after nonlinear excitations disperse.
conclusion: This framework enables analysis of driven photonic systems whose topology depends on finite-time dynamics rather than an idealized Floquet cycle.

title: Transformers As Intrinsic Optimizers For Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
authors: Kuan-Cheng Chen, Xiaotian Xu, Hiromichi Matsuyama, Wei-Hao Huang, Haomu Yuan, Yu Yamashiro
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a leading variational framework for combinatorial optimization on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware, but its practical performance depends strongly on the classical optimizer used to train its variational parameters. This outer-loop optimization is often nonconvex, initialization-sensitive, and costly when repeated across large families of related problem instances. In this work, we propose a Transformer-based intrinsic optimization framework for QAOA, in which the optimizer itself is learned and embedded directly into the hybrid quantum-classical loop. The proposed graph-conditioned Transformer processes problem structure, current QAOA parameters, measurement feedback, and recent optimization history to predict the next variational-parameter update, thereby reformulating instance-wise classical optimization as an amortized learned policy. We develop a mathematical formulation of this intrinsic-optimization perspective and evaluate the method on QAOA-based MaxCut benchmarks across multiple problem settings, with comparisons against representative classical and learned optimization baselines. The results demonstrate that Transformer-based intrinsic optimization can provide a structured and transferable mechanism for improving the classical component of hybrid quantum optimization algorithms.
tldr: The paper proposes a Transformer-based learned optimizer that predicts QAOA variational-parameter updates directly within the hybrid quantum-classical loop, amortizing instance-wise classical optimization.
motivation: QAOA performance depends strongly on the outer-loop classical optimizer, which is typically nonconvex, initialization-sensitive, and expensive to rerun across many related problem instances.
method: A graph-conditioned Transformer ingests problem structure, current QAOA parameters, measurement feedback, and recent optimization history to output the next parameter update, effectively learning a transferable optimization policy for QAOA.
result: On QAOA-based MaxCut benchmarks across multiple settings, the Transformer-based intrinsic optimizer compares favorably against representative classical and learned optimization baselines.
conclusion: Learned amortized optimization can provide a structured and transferable mechanism for improving the classical component of hybrid quantum optimization algorithms, though the work is algorithmically rather than physically or information-theoretically focused.

title: Limits On The Free-space Group Velocity Of Optical Wave Packets Incorporating Angular Dispersion. Part~II, Non-differentiable Angular Dispersion: Tutorial
authors: Ayman F. Abouraddy Layton A. Hall
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In Part~I of this tutorial, we showed that introducing angular dispersion (AD) into a collimated optical pulse allows for tuning the wave packet group velocity in free space. In principle, the group velocity can take on arbitrary values, whether superluminal, subluminal, or even negative. However, any significant deviation of the group velocity from [MATH] (the speed of light in vacuum) necessitates propagation at large angles with respect to the optical axis in the non-paraxial regime. In Part~II of this tutorial, we describe the recent discovery of a new form of AD we refer to as `non-differentiable AD', which circumvents the limits imposed by conventional (differentiable) AD. Non-differentiable AD does refer to an AD profile that is discontinuous, contains a kink, or features a singularity. Rather, a non-differentiable AD profile is continuous, smooth, and is differentiable everywhere except for one wavelength at which the derivative is not defined. We show that salutary features follow from this non-differentiability with respect to tuning the group velocity of a pulsed beam in free space; namely, significant deviations in the group velocity away from [MATH] are achievable in the paraxial regime while remaining free of group-velocity dispersion and all higher-order dispersive effects. This tutorial presents an outline of these recent results for tuning the group velocity of a wave packet via non-differentiable AD, connecting them with the corresponding results associated with conventional AD -- as outlined in Part~I. Moreover, we show that non-differentiable AD undergirds the unique characteristics of propagation-invariant space-time wave packets, thus unifying a large swathe of results in a single conceptual framework.
tldr: A tutorial (Part II) describing 'non-differentiable angular dispersion' as a means to tune the free-space group velocity of space-time optical wave packets in the paraxial regime without introducing group-velocity dispersion.
motivation: Part I showed that conventional (differentiable) angular dispersion can tune a wave packet's group velocity in free space, but large deviations from c require non-paraxial propagation. This work seeks a route to large group-velocity tunability while remaining paraxial and dispersion-free.
method: The authors introduce and analyze angular-dispersion profiles that are continuous and smooth but have an undefined derivative at a single wavelength, and connect these to propagation-invariant space-time wave packet behavior within a unified conceptual framework.
result: Non-differentiable angular dispersion permits significant deviations of the group velocity from c in the paraxial regime, free of group-velocity dispersion and higher-order dispersive effects, and explains the properties of propagation-invariant space-time wave packets.
conclusion: Non-differentiable angular dispersion circumvents the limits of conventional angular dispersion and unifies a broad class of space-time wave packet results, providing new design principles for classical free-space optical pulse propagation.

title: Polynomial-Time Mimo Detection At The Maximum-Likelihood Threshold
authors: Dimitris Papailiopoulos
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19405v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that exact block recovery in the square Gaussian binary MIMO model can be achieved in polynomial time at the same first-order SNR threshold as exhaustive maximum-likelihood detection. Specifically, for [MATH] and independent standard Gaussian [MATH] and [MATH], rounded linear MMSE followed by steepest single-bit descent recovers [MATH] with failure probability tending to zero, uniformly over every transmitted word and every [MATH], using [MATH] unit-cost exact-real arithmetic operations. The model is a special case of Gaussian random linear estimation, for which AMP state evolution and replica/MMSE formulas rigorously characterize fixed-parameter normalized performance. Those results predict the same [MATH] scale, but do not by themselves yield an all-coordinate guarantee in the dimension-dependent regime considered here. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work gives polynomial-time exact block recovery at the ML boundary for this setting; the closest prior square-system theorem, for the box relaxation, has first-order threshold [MATH]. The proof places the rounded LMMSE estimate at sublinear Hamming distance from the truth, and then establishes, uniformly over every error set the local search can visit, that some wrong bit offers a quantified cost decrease while an objective barrier confines the search path. Conversely, if [MATH] with [MATH] and [MATH], then a one-bit neighbor beats the transmitted word with probability tending to one, so even ML detection fails. Therefore, the statistical and polynomial-time exact-recovery thresholds coincide to first order in the stated arithmetic model.
tldr: Proves polynomial-time exact block recovery for square Gaussian binary MIMO at the maximum-likelihood SNR threshold using rounded LMMSE and steepest single-bit descent.
motivation: MIMO detection seeks efficient algorithms matching optimal ML performance, and this work addresses whether polynomial-time exact recovery can be achieved at the ML threshold in a Gaussian random linear estimation model.
method: Analyzes rounded linear MMSE followed by steepest single-bit descent, using sublinear Hamming distance initialization and a local-search barrier argument; connects to AMP state evolution and replica/MMSE predictions.
result: Shows failure probability tends to zero uniformly over transmitted words and SNR when system size grows, with the same first-order threshold as ML; also shows ML fails below threshold, so statistical and polynomial-time exact-recovery thresholds coincide.
conclusion: In the stated arithmetic model, exact block recovery is possible in polynomial time at the ML boundary, closing a gap with prior box-relaxation thresholds.

title: Reconstructability Of Inverse Problems Under Symmetry: Separating Structural, Effective, And Physical Upper Bounds
authors: Isshin Arai
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In our previous work we introduced the Reconstruction Dimension, an upper bound on the reconstructable degrees of freedom determined solely by the symmetry. In actual physical systems, however, the state quantities are generated through physical processes [MATH] induced by the cause [MATH]. The state space is therefore often degenerate, and the upper bound determined by the representation-theoretic structure is not reached. This calls for a distinction between the upper bound determined solely by symmetry and the one realized after the physical process. We therefore introduce a three-level structure of upper bounds: the Structural, Effective, and Physical Reconstruction Dimensions (SRD, ERD, PRD), determined respectively by the representation-theoretic structure of the intermediate space, by the concrete design of the reconstruction map, and by the degeneracy of the state space under the physical process [MATH]. For each irreducible component they form the hierarchy [MATH], so that the two gaps identify at which level reconstructability is lost. The framework is illustrated through two contrasting systems: the orientation dynamics of flake-like particles, where the cause is a velocity gradinet, and the two-body problem, where the cause itself is defined through the symmetry. This paper provides a concrete framework for reconstruction in physical inverse problems.
tldr: Introduces a three-level hierarchy of reconstruction dimensions—structural, effective, and physical—for inverse problems under symmetry, distinguishing symmetry-based bounds from physically realized reconstructability.
motivation: Prior work defined a reconstruction dimension from symmetry alone, but physical systems often have degenerate state spaces, so the representation-theoretic upper bound is not reached.
method: Defines structural, effective, and physical reconstruction dimensions via representation theory, the concrete reconstruction map, and degeneracy from physical processes, illustrated with flake orientation dynamics and the two-body problem.
result: The hierarchy reveals gaps between structural and effective bounds (due to map design) and between effective and physical bounds (due to physical degeneracy), pinpointing where reconstructability is lost.
conclusion: Provides a framework for analyzing reconstruction limits in physical inverse problems, separating symmetry-imposed bounds from those realized after the physical process.

title: Rapidity-Coupled Spin Dynamics In Pulsed Laser Fields From Physics-Informed Neural Networks
authors: N. S. Akintsov, A. P. Nevecheria, S. N. Andreev, Qing-Hua Qin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Carrier-envelope-phase (CEP) stabilized few-cycle pulses make the sub-cycle field structure a control parameter for laser-driven polarized electron sources, yet spin solvers for such pulses are rarely tested against exact results. We show that for an electron initially at rest in a linearly polarized plane-wave pulse the rest-frame polarization angle follows the instantaneous vector potential, [MATH] with [MATH] the electron anomaly: the net rotation vanishes for every CEP, while the peak intra-pulse angle varies over the CEP by 3.02 degrees for a two-cycle and by 0.22 degrees for an eight-cycle pulse. The result follows from the Volkov orbit in longitudinal and transverse rapidities. We use it to validate a light-front reference integrator and a physics-informed neural network trained only on the light-front equations, which reaches [MATH] in the spin sector and carries over to elliptical polarization, for which no closed-form solution is known. This gives validated tools for CEP-resolved spin dynamics in intense fields.
tldr: The paper derives an exact relation between the rest-frame polarization angle of an initially at-rest electron and the instantaneous vector potential in a few-cycle laser pulse, and uses it to validate a light-front integrator and a physics-informed neural network for CEP-resolved spin dynamics.
motivation: Carrier-envelope-phase-stabilized few-cycle pulses make sub-cycle field structure a control knob for laser-driven polarized electron sources, but numerical spin solvers for such pulses are rarely benchmarked against exact solvable results.
method: The authors solve the Volkov orbit in longitudinal and transverse rapidities to obtain a closed-form spin/polarization rotation, then train a physics-informed neural network on the light-front spin equations and compare its predictions to the exact solution and to a light-front reference integrator.
result: The rest-frame polarization angle tracks the instantaneous vector potential scaled by the electron anomaly, giving zero net rotation for all CEP values, while the peak intra-pulse angle varies by 3.02 degrees for a two-cycle pulse and 0.22 degrees for an eight-cycle pulse; the PINN achieves accurate spin-sector predictions and generalizes to elliptical polarization where no closed form exists.
conclusion: The work provides validated numerical tools for CEP-resolved spin dynamics in intense laser fields, with potential relevance to polarized electron source design.

title: Source Entropy-Guided Adaptive Transmission For Communication-Driven Multi-View Sensing
authors: Mingjie Yang, Guangming Liang, Dongzhu Liu, Lei Zhang, Xiaonan Liu, Kaibin Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Communication-driven multi-view sensing relies on routine communication transmissions for sensing acquisition, while the resulting sensing data at distributed devices must be uploaded to an edge server under limited communication resources. This creates a unique coupling between sensing acquisition and edge inference: the communication interval determines the source information, whereas the uplink condition determines how much information can be delivered to the server for sensing inference. To account for this coupling, we propose a source entropy-guided adaptive transmission framework. Specifically, we characterize the entropy of packet-triggered channel state information (CSI) as a function of the communication interval using a multi-output Gaussian process. The resulting analytical bound is compared with the available bit budget, determined by the transmission rate and latency requirement, to select between original-data and task-oriented transmission. For task-oriented transmission, we formulate the communication-constrained inference problem based on the information bottleneck and decompose it into adaptive distributed encoding and multi-view inference (ADE-MI), which avoids alternating optimization between the devices and the edge server. Experiments on the Widar3.0 multi-view CSI gesture recognition dataset show that the analytical bound closely follows the normalizing-flow numerical estimate, while ADE-MI outperforms task-oriented benchmarks under the same bit budget and the proposed framework further improves recognition accuracy under time-varying channels.
tldr: This paper proposes a source entropy-guided adaptive transmission framework for communication-driven multi-view sensing, selecting between original-data and task-oriented transmission based on entropy bounds and bit budgets.
motivation: Communication-driven multi-view sensing couples sensing acquisition with edge inference, since the communication interval determines the source information while the uplink condition limits the amount of information available for inference.
method: The authors model packet-triggered CSI entropy using a multi-output Gaussian process, compare the analytical bound with the available bit budget, and decompose a communication-constrained inference problem based on the information bottleneck into adaptive distributed encoding and multi-view inference.
result: Experiments on the Widar3.0 multi-view CSI gesture recognition dataset show the analytical bound closely follows a normalizing-flow numerical estimate, and the proposed ADE-MI method outperforms task-oriented benchmarks under the same bit budget.
conclusion: The framework improves recognition accuracy under time-varying channels and demonstrates the benefit of source entropy-guided transmission for communication-driven multi-view sensing.

title: A Generalization Of The Map $\chi$
authors: Xiutao Feng, Qiang Wang, Jingyi Yu, Anpeng Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The mapping [MATH] defined by [MATH] with [MATH], where the indices are computed modulo [MATH], has been widely studied for its application in lightweight cryptography. In this paper, we generalize this mapping and completely characterize all these shift-invariant permutations of algebraic degree [MATH].
tldr: The paper generalizes the cryptographic map χ and completely characterizes all shift-invariant permutations of a given algebraic degree.
motivation: The map χ is widely used in lightweight cryptography, and understanding its generalizations and structural properties can aid in designing or analyzing cryptographic primitives.
method: The authors generalize the mapping χ and provide a complete algebraic characterization of all shift-invariant permutations with specified algebraic degree, using combinatorial and algebraic techniques.
result: They completely classify all shift-invariant permutations of algebraic degree under the generalized map, extending known results for the original χ mapping.
conclusion: This work contributes to the mathematical foundations of lightweight cryptography but has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Boundary Parity In The Mirror Model On The Manhattan Lattice
authors: Qin Hao Jian Gu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19498v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a finite-domain event for the mirror model on the Manhattan lattice: every boundary-to-boundary trajectory crosses a marked connector an even number of times, while internal cycles are unrestricted. Our main theorem gives a finite-scale confinement criterion: if this event's probability reaches a universal threshold in one even two-square rectangle, then almost surely every trajectory in the plane is periodic. We construct an exactly normalized three-color tensor representation and prove deterministic bounds for approximate contractions using the signed partial-permutation structure of directed continuations. These tools turn numerical evaluations into rigorous finite-volume statements. At mirror density \(p=2/5\), we prove that the boundary-parity probability is nonmonotone in the rectangle width, with a decrease followed by a certified increase. These values remain below the sufficient confinement threshold and do not resolve planar localization at this density. Further experiments track how the measured finite-size minimum varies with density, compare matching-based and entrywise error bounds, and exhibit endpoint-sensitive and cooperative responses to local mirror changes.
tldr: The paper studies a boundary-parity event in the mirror model on the Manhattan lattice and provides a finite-scale confinement criterion for planar periodicity.
motivation: The authors aim to understand when boundary-to-boundary trajectories in the mirror model become confined or periodic, and to link finite-volume numerical evidence to rigorous statements.
method: They construct an exactly normalized three-color tensor representation and prove deterministic bounds for approximate contractions using the signed partial-permutation structure of directed continuations.
result: At mirror density p=2/5, the boundary-parity probability is shown to be nonmonotone in rectangle width, with a decrease followed by a certified increase, but remains below the sufficient confinement threshold.
conclusion: The tools turn numerical evaluations into rigorous finite-volume statements, yet they do not resolve planar localization at p=2/5.

title: Eberlein Convolution As An Inner Product And Quantitative Bombieri--Taylor Results
authors: Nicolae Strungaru Daniel Lenz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19501v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a simple argument providing a very general Bombieri--Taylor-type result to compute Bragg peaks in diffraction theory as limits. At its abstract core the argument relies on considering the Eberlein convolution as an inner product. This inner product gives an abstract version of a Cauchy--Schwarz type inequality which implies the Bombieri--Taylor-type result as well as generalizations.
tldr: The paper presents a general Bombieri-Taylor-type result for computing Bragg peaks in diffraction theory by treating the Eberlein convolution as an inner product.
motivation: Bragg peaks are important in diffraction theory, and existing Bombieri-Taylor results can be extended via a more abstract and general argument.
method: The authors interpret the Eberlein convolution as an inner product and derive an abstract Cauchy-Schwarz-type inequality from it.
result: This inequality implies a very general Bombieri-Taylor-type result for Bragg peaks as limits, along with further generalizations.
conclusion: The approach provides a simple, abstract framework for quantitative results in diffraction theory, but it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Projections And Minimal Invariant Subspaces In The Hardy Space Over The Bidisk
authors: Jo\~ao Marcos Ribeiro Do Carmo Marcos Dos Santos Ferreira
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19311v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the rigidity of the orthogonal projections [MATH], where [MATH] and each [MATH] is a reducing subspace for [MATH], and we derive properties of the minimal invariant subspaces of [MATH]. Our main result establishes that the nonzero projections of a minimal invariant subspace onto the one-variable Hardy space share a common [MATH]-invariant structure. Furthermore, we relate the results obtained to an approach to the invariant subspace problem.
tldr: The paper studies orthogonal projections and minimal invariant subspaces in the Hardy space over the bidisk, relating the results to the invariant subspace problem.
motivation: The authors aim to understand the structure of reducing subspaces and minimal invariant subspaces in a multivariable Hardy space setting.
method: They analyze orthogonal projections onto one-variable Hardy spaces and derive common invariant structure for nonzero projections of minimal invariant subspaces.
result: The main result shows that projections of a minimal invariant subspace onto the one-variable Hardy space share a common invariant structure, with connections to the invariant subspace problem.
conclusion: The work provides structural insights into invariant subspaces in the bidisk Hardy space, though it is purely mathematical and unrelated to quantum information.

title: Affine Quantum Schur--Weyl Duality
authors: Jun Hu Qiang Fu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19608v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] be an arbitrary commutative ring containing an invertible element [MATH]. Let [MATH] be the extended affine Hecke algebra of type [MATH] with Hecke parameter [MATH], let [MATH] be the affine tensor space, and let [MATH] be the corresponding affine quantum Schur algebra. We first prove that the natural right action of [MATH] on [MATH] is always faithful. Assume further that [MATH] is a field of characteristic [MATH] and that [MATH] is not a root of unity. We prove that, for any [MATH], the natural algebra homomorphism [MATH] is an isomorphism. This proves Conjecture~3.8.8 of . As an application, we prove the conjecture formulated in \cite[5.2.4]{DDF} concerning the center of the affine quantum Schur algebra. We also prove that [MATH] is left and right Noetherian whenever [MATH] is a Noetherian commutative ring, which verify a conjecture in \cite[Rem. 1.7]{DY}.
tldr: The paper proves affine quantum Schur-Weyl duality and related conjectures on the center and Noetherian property of affine quantum Schur algebras.
motivation: Affine quantum Schur algebras and their duality with extended affine Hecke algebras are central in algebraic representation theory, with conjectures remaining open about the faithfulness of natural actions, isomorphism of homomorphisms, and algebraic properties.
method: The authors use representation-theoretic and algebraic techniques for extended affine Hecke algebras and affine tensor spaces over commutative rings and fields of characteristic not dividing certain parameters, proving faithfulness and isomorphism, and deriving center and Noetherian results.
result: They show the natural right action is faithful, the natural algebra homomorphism is an isomorphism under characteristic-zero assumptions, proving Conjecture 3.8.8, and they verify conjectures on the center and on left/right Noetherianity.
conclusion: The work resolves several conjectures in the theory of affine quantum Schur algebras, advancing pure algebraic representation theory but having no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Fictitious Domain Formulation With Bubble Enrichment
authors: Stefano Berrone, Lorenzo Neva, Stefano Scial\`o, Fabio Vicini
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The fictitious domain method offers a powerful alternative to circumvent complex mesh generation process by embedding the complex physical domain into a simpler, non-matching background mesh. Among the various strategies to enforce the boundary condition on such a mesh, one possibility is to impose it weakly through a Lagrange multiplier. Existing approaches following this strategy typically require two independent uniform meshes for the domain and the boundary, whose mesh sizes are related by a prescribed ratio. In this work, we relax this requirement by constructing the boundary mesh directly from the trace of the background triangulation. To recover the uniform discrete inf-sup condition under this weaker mesh assumption, we enrich the discrete space of the solution with bubble functions. Our main result is the construction of a suitable operator that allows us to prove this uniform discrete inf-sup condition, thereby establishing the stability of the resulting scheme. As a consequence, we derive optimal a priori error estimates and provide a numerical experiment to validate the theoretical results.
tldr: The paper develops a fictitious domain method with Lagrange multipliers and bubble enrichment to weakly enforce boundary conditions on non-matching meshes.
motivation: Fictitious domain methods avoid complex mesh generation, but existing Lagrange multiplier approaches require two independent uniform meshes with a prescribed mesh-size ratio.
method: The boundary mesh is constructed from the trace of the background triangulation, and bubble functions are added to the discrete solution space to recover the uniform discrete inf-sup condition.
result: The authors prove the uniform discrete inf-sup condition, establishing stability and deriving optimal a priori error estimates, validated by a numerical experiment.
conclusion: The proposed enrichment enables stable fictitious domain discretizations under weaker mesh assumptions, simplifying mesh generation while preserving optimal convergence.

title: Percolation Markov Decision Processes
authors: Guillaume Vigeral Melissa Gonz\'alez Garc\'ia (CES)
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19905v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study Percolation Markov Decision Processes (PMDPs), in which the decision maker repeatedly moves a token through the d-dimensional integer lattice with deterministic transitions and random payoffs assigned to the edges. Payoffs are revealed before the beginning of the decision process and the decision maker aims to maximize the average accumulated payoff over a fixed horizon. We establish the existence of the uniform value (as the horizon tends to infinity) and 0-optimal strategies. In the particular case of Bernoulli payoffs, we establish continuity results for the uniform value. We also present several one-dimensional examples to illustrate that optimal strategies may be very complex. Then, we introduce a dimensional lifting property that allows PMDPs to be approximated by PMDPs of lower dimension and could be used to approximate critical probability thresholds in percolation theory.
tldr: The paper introduces Percolation Markov Decision Processes on the d-dimensional lattice with random edge payoffs and proves existence of uniform value, 0-optimal strategies, and a dimensional lifting property.
motivation: The authors aim to study stochastic control problems where a decision maker navigates a lattice with random rewards, connecting decision-process theory to percolation phenomena and critical thresholds.
method: They analyze deterministic transitions with random edge payoffs over a fixed horizon, establishing existence of the uniform value and 0-optimal strategies, and prove continuity results in the Bernoulli payoff case; one-dimensional examples illustrate complex optimal strategies, and a dimensional lifting property links high-dimensional PMDPs to lower-dimensional ones.
result: The uniform value exists and 0-optimal strategies are characterized, continuity of the uniform value holds under Bernoulli payoffs, and the lifting property enables approximation of critical probability thresholds in percolation theory.
conclusion: PMDPs provide a new framework bridging Markov decision processes and percolation theory, with the lifting property offering a potential tool for estimating critical thresholds.

title: Dynamics Of Stochastic Hamiltonian Systems I - Wong-Zakai Variational Integrators
authors: Rouba Safi Jacky Cresson (LMAP)
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct variational integrators to study the dynamics of stochastic Hamiltonian systems using their Wong-Zakai approximation. This approach can be used to interpret and justify previous work of Wang et al (L. Wang, J. Hong, R. Scherer, F. Bai. Dynamics and variational Integrators of stochastic Hamiltonian systems. International Journal of Numerical Analysis and Modeling, 6(4), 2009) on stochastic variational integrators. Numerical examples are provided.
tldr: The paper constructs variational integrators for stochastic Hamiltonian systems using the Wong-Zakai approximation.
motivation: To study the dynamics of stochastic Hamiltonian systems and provide a framework that interprets and justifies previous work on stochastic variational integrators.
method: The authors use the Wong-Zakai approximation to derive variational integrators for stochastic Hamiltonian systems.
result: Numerical examples demonstrate the behavior of the proposed integrators and support the theoretical construction.
conclusion: Variational integrators based on the Wong-Zakai approximation are effective tools for simulating stochastic Hamiltonian dynamics.

title: Revisiting The Brunner-Munzel Test From The Viewpoint Of Local Linear Approximation
authors: Makito Oku
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19986v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Brunner-Munzel (BM) test is a nonparametric test for two independent samples that evaluates whether observations from one group tend to be greater than observations from another group, or vice versa. The BM test has a broader scope of application than the Mann-Whitney [MATH] test because it does not assume equal variances between the two groups. However, the meaning of the BM test statistic is difficult to understand intuitively, which may be one of the factors hindering the widespread use of the BM test. To alleviate this problem, in this paper, I introduce an alternative interpretation of the BM test statistic from the viewpoint of local linear approximation. It is shown that the variance estimator for the sample stochastic superiority used in the BM test can be derived using local linear approximation, in which the influence of each observation on the sample stochastic superiority is assumed to be additive. This simple interpretation will help practitioners decide to use the BM test without hesitation.
tldr: The paper reinterprets the Brunner-Munzel nonparametric test statistic using local linear approximation to make its variance estimator more intuitive.
motivation: The Brunner-Munzel test is more general than the Mann-Whitney test but its test statistic is difficult to understand, which hinders its adoption by practitioners.
method: The author derives the variance estimator for the sample stochastic superiority via local linear approximation, assuming additive influence of each observation.
result: The BM test statistic's variance estimator is shown to arise naturally from a simple additive local linear approximation framework.
conclusion: This alternative interpretation clarifies the BM test and may encourage practitioners to use it without hesitation.

title: Strategyproof Aggregation In Euclidean Spaces: Rigidity And Median Optimality
authors: Jianhao Jia
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19394v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study deterministic strategyproof aggregation in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces. For every odd number [MATH] of agents and every finite dimension, we prove that the coordinate-wise median minimizes the worst-case approximation ratio for total Euclidean distance among all continuous, anonymous, deterministic strategyproof mechanisms. The same optimality result holds for every even [MATH] when each coordinate uses a fixed choice of the lower or upper middle rank. The proof combines a rigidity theorem with a normalization that does not increase the approximation ratio: any hypothetical mechanism outperforming the median has a normalized representative that is a fixed coordinate-wise order-statistic rule in a single orthonormal frame. A reflection argument then shows that no such rule improves on the median.
tldr: The paper proves that coordinate-wise median mechanisms are optimal (strategyproof, worst-case optimal) for minimizing total Euclidean distance in finite-dimensional aggregation problems.
motivation: Deterministic strategyproof aggregation in Euclidean spaces is a fundamental problem in social choice and mechanism design, where the optimal approximation ratio of simple mechanisms like the median was not fully characterized.
method: The authors combine a rigidity theorem with a normalization argument showing any superior mechanism has a normalized representative that is a coordinate-wise order-statistic rule in a single orthonormal frame, then apply a reflection argument.
result: The coordinate-wise median minimizes the worst-case approximation ratio for total Euclidean distance among all continuous, anonymous, deterministic strategyproof mechanisms for odd numbers of agents, with an analogous result for even numbers.
conclusion: Median-based aggregation is optimal in the worst-case Euclidean sense, establishing sharp performance guarantees for strategyproof mechanisms and reinforcing the median's privileged role in Euclidean mechanism design.

title: Reachability, Not Observation: Containing Systems Whose Wiring Changes
authors: Yoshiaki Takashita
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Containment decisions -- where to put a firewall, which links to monitor, what a program may reach -- are computed from an observed structure, and observation is a snapshot. We ask what a snapshot misses when the wiring changes over time. On a hypercube whose active dimension rotates, a balanced split shows zero crossing edges at 93% of instants, yet 8,192 edges must be blocked permanently; adding one always-on ring, a defender sees 2 where 8,194 must be blocked, a factor of 4,097. A time-aware defender holds 585 blocks on average, but one step of clock lag drops its containment to 0%. On the real Internet the same gap is only x1.8-2.0 (1997-2000) and x1.5-1.6 (2024-2026) once growth is removed, so the blind spot is introduced by design, not inherited from the world -- and it has been designed: the round-robin schedules of optical datacentre fabrics have a gap equal to their period. A declared capability map, checked by static reachability over a real application's call graph, catches all 8 planted holes; the string deny-list previously in place catches 2. One calculation generates every number from one parameter, the period, and reads three boundaries not usually called schedules: frequency hopping, whose standard results are these closed forms with channels in place of edges; the air gap, whose always-on crossing set is empty and whose known breach came at the one phase a snapshot misses; and the tool surface of a coding agent, inventoried from the inside. Turning the cuts on that agent: idle, its instantaneous state cut is zero, while 6 channels carry it across a context reset, none of them the network, so severing the network removes 0. The channel that spawns copies is a branching process with a sharp threshold at approval rate 1/b, below which denial is unnecessary and above which denial is insufficient. Contain by the paths that exist, not by the behaviour that was seen.
tldr: The paper analyzes how snapshot-based containment decisions fail when network wiring changes over time, using hypercube rotations, optical datacenter fabrics, frequency hopping, air gaps, and coding-agent tool surfaces as examples.
motivation: Containment decisions such as firewall placement, link monitoring, and program reachability are typically computed from a single observed structure, but real systems change their wiring over time, so snapshots may miss critical reachable paths.
method: The authors model changing-wiring scenarios mathematically, including a hypercube with rotating active dimension, a time-aware defender with clock lag, round-robin optical datacenter schedules, and static reachability over an application call graph to detect planted holes.
result: A balanced split on a rotating hypercube shows zero crossing edges at 93% of instants while 8,192 edges must be permanently blocked; adding an always-on ring creates a defender blind spot factor of 4,097; one step of clock lag drops containment to 0%; and a capability map catches all 8 planted holes versus 2 for a string deny-list.
conclusion: Containment should be based on paths that exist over time rather than observed behavior, because the blind spot is often introduced by design, as seen in datacenter schedules, frequency hopping, air gaps, and coding-agent tool surfaces.

title: Exact Regret Frontiers And Externality Scheduling In Centralized Serial-Dictatorship Bandits
authors: Lishang Xu, Guodong Ma, Pengcheng Weng, Zixuan Xia
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19963v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exploration in centralized serial-dictatorship matching bandits must use complete matchings, so learning one player--arm pair can impose regret on others. We study this externality under a known common priority order and Gaussian rewards with unit variance. We show that the matching-level Graves--Lai constraints reduce to finitely many pairwise exploration quotas and, at top-choice-separated instances, yield a polynomial-size marginal linear program. At these instances, the exact attainable set of expected logarithmic regret coefficients is [MATH], where [MATH] is the feasible matching-allocation set and [MATH] maps allocations to player regret. The usual upper-closed Graves--Lai region can be strictly larger despite having the same Pareto-minimal boundary. We further show that identical exploration quotas can induce very different regret through their scheduling. Finally, we construct estimate--solve--track policies, uniformly good on the full row-strict class, that attain every fixed positively weighted optimum without assuming optimizer uniqueness. Every Pareto-minimal point is pointwise attainable, possibly through an instance-calibrated target.
tldr: The paper characterizes the exact attainable frontier of expected logarithmic regret coefficients in centralized serial-dictatorship matching bandits and shows scheduling of exploration quotas substantially affects regret.
motivation: Exploration in a centralized serial-dictatorship matching bandit requires complete matchings, so learning one player-arm pair imposes externalities (regret) on other players; the authors aim to characterize this externality exactly.
method: Assuming a known common priority order and unit-variance Gaussian rewards, they reduce matching-level Graves-Lai constraints to finitely many pairwise exploration quotas, derive a polynomial-size marginal linear program at top-choice-separated instances, and construct estimate-solve-track policies.
result: The attainable set of expected logarithmic regret coefficients is exactly the image of the feasible matching-allocation set under a regret map; identical exploration quotas can yield very different regret due to scheduling, and every Pareto-minimal point is pointwise attainable.
conclusion: The work provides exact regret frontiers and shows scheduling is a first-class design lever, with uniformly good policies over the full row-strict class attaining every fixed positively weighted optimum.

title: A Closed-Form Molecule-Release Rule For Diffusion-Based Molecular Communications With Ligand Receptors
authors: Murat Kuscu Eren Kural
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20023v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The number of molecules released per bit is a fundamental design variable of diffusion-based molecular communication (MC), and ligand-receptor reception breaks the more-is-better intuition.
