Too few molecules leave the bound-receptor observations buried in binding noise, while too many amplify the accumulated intersymbol interference and saturate the finite receptor population, again making the observations indistinguishable. Reliability therefore peaks in an interior operating region whose location seems to require an exhaustive search over the channel dynamics. In this paper, we show that this search can be obviated for a biologically plausible receiver that compares consecutive bound-receptor counts without channel state information or a decision threshold. We derive a closed-form transmission rule, which sets the number of molecules released per bit such that the receptor dissociation constant equals the geometric mean of the two bit-conditioned received concentration levels, prove that it exactly minimizes the bit error probability of a memoryless binomial receptor model, and express it in the physical channel parameters through an Euler--Maclaurin evaluation of the interference. Time-domain Monte Carlo sweeps of the channel and receptor parameters, corroborated by particle-based simulations, show that the empirically optimal release count coincides with the prediction or lies above it by a small factor.
tldr: A closed-form rule for the number of molecules released per bit in diffusion-based molecular communication with ligand receptors is derived to minimize bit error probability without exhaustive search.
motivation: The number of released molecules per bit is a key design variable in molecular communication, but ligand-receptor reception creates a trade-off between binding noise and intersymbol interference, making reliability peak at an interior optimum that typically requires costly search over channel dynamics.
method: The authors derive a closed-form transmission rule for a memoryless binomial receptor model by setting the receptor dissociation constant equal to the geometric mean of the two bit-conditioned received concentration levels, and they evaluate interference using an Euler–Maclaurin expansion.
result: The rule exactly minimizes the bit error probability of the memoryless binomial receptor model, and time-domain Monte Carlo sweeps plus particle-based simulations show the empirically optimal release count matches or slightly exceeds the prediction.
conclusion: A simple closed-form release rule eliminates the need for exhaustive search in diffusion-based molecular communication with ligand receptors, providing a practical design guideline for biologically plausible receivers.

title: Femtoscopic Correlation Functions In Density Operator Representation
authors: Hao-Nan Liu, Duo-Lun Ge, Zhi-Wei Liu, Jun-Xu Lu, Li-Sheng Geng
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Femtoscopic correlation functions (CFs) have been increasingly used to extract strong interactions between pairs of unstable particles, but their physical soundness has recently been questioned. To answer this, we formulate CFs at the operator level, with the observed subsystem described by a reduced density operator and subsequent dynamics absorbed into an effective measurement operator. The Koonin-Pratt form is recovered under four well-motivated reductions. The formulation makes explicit that the source-side and interaction-side representations must be consistently matched, and motivates an operational convention in which a measured reference correlation establishes a compatible source--interaction pairing that can be extended to other pairs for CF-to-CF predictions.
tldr: The paper reformulates femtoscopic correlation functions using a reduced density operator and effective measurement operator, recovering the Koonin-Pratt form under specific reductions.
motivation: Femtoscopic correlation functions are widely used to extract strong interactions between unstable particle pairs, but their physical soundness has been questioned.
method: The authors formulate correlation functions at the operator level, describing the observed subsystem by a reduced density operator and absorbing subsequent dynamics into an effective measurement operator.
result: They recover the Koonin-Pratt form under four well-motivated reductions and show that source-side and interaction-side representations must be consistently matched.
conclusion: The work motivates an operational convention where a measured reference correlation establishes a compatible source-interaction pairing extendable to other pairs for CF-to-CF predictions.

title: The Spectral $\zeta$-function Of Sturm--Liouville Operators With $n$ Generalized Point Potentials
authors: Jonathan Stanfill Guglielmo Fucci
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19322v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work analyzes the spectral zeta function associated with regular and singular Sturm--Liouville operators endowed with [MATH] generalized point potentials. The point interactions are characterized as a particular class of self-adjoint extensions of Sturm--Liouville operators defined on a chain of [MATH] adjacent intervals. Each interaction is described by [MATH] matching conditions relating generalized boundary values across neighboring intervals. We construct the spectral zeta function associated with Sturm--Liouville operators endowed with [MATH] generalized point potentials in terms of a contour integral involving an appropriate characteristic function. The process of analytic continuation of the spectral zeta function to a neighborhood of the origin is illustrated by means of specific examples where the [MATH]-regularized functional determinant is also explicitly computed.
tldr: The paper constructs and analytically continues the spectral zeta function for regular and singular Sturm-Liouville operators carrying n generalized point potentials, using a contour-integral representation of the characteristic function.
motivation: Spectral zeta functions and regularized functional determinants are central tools in spectral geometry and mathematical physics, and extending them to operators with generalized point interactions (self-adjoint extensions on chains of adjacent intervals) is of interest for handling singular configurations.
method: The point interactions are modeled as matching conditions on generalized boundary values across n adjacent intervals, and the spectral zeta function is expressed as a contour integral of a characteristic function, with analytic continuation to the origin performed via worked examples.
result: Explicit analytic continuation of the spectral zeta function near the origin is illustrated for specific examples, and the corresponding zeta-regularized functional determinants are computed in closed form.
conclusion: The framework provides a systematic route to zeta-function and functional-determinant computations for Sturm-Liouville problems with multiple generalized point potentials, extending standard spectral techniques to singular point-interaction settings.

title: Limits On The Free-space Group Velocity Of Optical Wave Packets Incorporating Angular Dispersion. Part~I, Conventional Angular Dispersion: Tutorial
authors: Ayman F. Abouraddy Layton A. Hall
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A plane-wave optical pulse travels in free space at a group velocity [MATH] (the speed of light in vacuum) measured along its propagation axis. It is sometimes thought that spatially structuring the field in free space reduces the group velocity below [MATH] because -- intuitively -- the oblique wave vectors undergirding the wave packet increase the average group delay. Here we show that spatiotemporally structuring a pulsed optical beam (or wave packet) can yield -- in principle -- arbitrary group velocities in free space in contradistinction to this commonly held intuition. We devote our attention here to pulses endowed with angular dispersion (AD) where the propagation angle is wavelength dependent. This class of wave packets is particularly pertinent because their group velocity is constant over the transverse field profile and along the propagation axis, thereby yielding an unambiguous group delay. However, significant deviation of the AD-induced group velocity in free space from~[MATH] inevitably requires a large numerical aperture that lies deep in the non-paraxial regime, and such wave packets experience AD-induced group-velocity dispersion. The formulation presented here captures a broad range of results, connecting them in a single framework. In Part~II of this tutorial, we describe recently identified `non-differentiable AD' (associated with propagation-invariant space-time wave packets) that helps circumvent the limits associated with conventional (differentiable) AD as outlined here.
tldr: This tutorial analyzes limits on the free-space group velocity of optical wave packets with conventional angular dispersion and shows that spatiotemporal structuring can in principle yield arbitrary group velocities.
motivation: It is commonly assumed that spatially structuring an optical pulse in free space reduces its group velocity below c due to oblique wave vectors, and this work aims to clarify and quantify that intuition.
method: The authors develop a framework for pulsed optical beams with wavelength-dependent propagation angle (angular dispersion) and analyze group velocity and group-velocity dispersion in the non-paraxial regime.
result: They show that significant deviations from c require large numerical apertures deep in the non-paraxial regime, where conventional angular dispersion also introduces group-velocity dispersion.
conclusion: The formulation unifies a broad range of results and sets the stage for Part II on non-differentiable angular dispersion in propagation-invariant space-time wave packets.

title: Skein Theory And Deformations
authors: Benjamin Spencer Noah Snyder
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We use skein theoretic `recognition' theorems to classify deformations of certain pivotal or ribbon monoidal categories. We first show that a slight generalization of Kuperberg's characterization of quantum [MATH] shows that any infinitesimal deformation of quantum [MATH] as a pivotal category arises by varying [MATH]. This result applies both at generic [MATH], and for the category of tilting modules at [MATH] a root of unity (provided we exclude a few small roots of unity). Second, we prove a new Kuperberg-like characterization of Deligne's [MATH] and use it to show that any infinitesimal deformation of [MATH] (excluding [MATH]) as a ribbon category comes from varying [MATH].
tldr: The paper uses skein-theoretic recognition theorems to classify infinitesimal deformations of pivotal and ribbon monoidal categories, including quantum groups and Deligne's category.
motivation: Understanding whether certain monoidal categories are rigid under deformation is a fundamental question in quantum algebra and topology.
method: The authors generalize Kuperberg's characterization of quantum groups and prove a new Kuperberg-like characterization of Deligne's category to analyze infinitesimal deformations.
result: They show that any infinitesimal deformation of quantum groups as a pivotal category arises by varying the parameter, both generically and at roots of unity (excluding small roots), and similarly for Deligne's category as a ribbon category.
conclusion: These recognition theorems provide a complete classification of deformations for the considered categories, confirming their rigidity up to parameter variation.

title: Deep Learning For Singular PDEs: A Weighted Neural Network Approach
authors: Badr Oulgiht
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19335v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a deep learning framework for the numerical approximation of weakly singular semilinear elliptic equations subject to homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and positivity constraints. These problems are challenging because the nonlinear source term becomes unbounded as the positive solution approaches zero near the boundary. The proposed approach combines three components. First, the Dirichlet boundary conditions are embedded directly into the neural representation through a hard-constraint formulation. Second, a Softplus transformation preserves positivity in the interior of the computational domain, ensuring that the singular nonlinear term remains well-defined during training. Third, a singularity-aware weighted residual loss emphasizes regions where the predicted solution becomes small and the singular behavior is more pronounced. The method is evaluated in the weak singularity regime through numerical reference solutions and controlled verification tests. Comparisons with the standard residual formulation are used to assess approximation accuracy and convergence behavior. The numerical experiments illustrate the potential of combining hard boundary enforcement, positivity preservation, and singularity-aware residual weighting for weakly singular elliptic problems.
tldr: The paper proposes a deep learning framework using hard-constrained boundary enforcement, Softplus positivity transforms, and a singularity-aware weighted residual loss to numerically approximate weakly singular semilinear elliptic PDEs.
motivation: Weakly singular semilinear elliptic equations with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and positivity constraints are hard to solve numerically because the nonlinear source term diverges as the solution vanishes near the boundary.
method: The authors embed Dirichlet boundary conditions directly into the neural representation, enforce interior positivity via a Softplus transformation, and use a singularity-aware weighted residual loss that emphasizes regions where the predicted solution is small.
result: Numerical experiments in the weak singularity regime, compared against standard residual formulations, show improved approximation accuracy and convergence behavior.
conclusion: Combining hard boundary enforcement, positivity preservation, and singularity-aware residual weighting shows potential for solving weakly singular elliptic problems.

title: Braided Hopf Algebroids And Lie Algebroids
authors: Xiao Han
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct braided Hopf algebroids in a braided monoidal category over a field [MATH] and study its properties using graphical representation. Then we study Ehresmann-Schauenburg Hopf algebroids assocaited to braided Hopf Galois extensions. We introduce braided Lie-Rinehart algebras which generalize the definition in and study its universal enveloping algebra under symmetric condition. In particular, we introduce Lie-Rinehart algebras (braided Lie-algebroids) associated with braided Hopf algebroids in the category of the module of a triangular Hopf algebra. We then focus on the case for braided Ehresmann-Schauenburg Hopf algebroids and study their right invariant vector fields, which turn out to be isomorphic to the [MATH]-equivariant vector fields on the quantum principal bundle (Hopf Galois extension) as Lie-Rinehart algebras. Finally, we introduce braided jet Hopf algebroids associate to braided Hopf algebroids in the case that the source and target subalgebra belong to the braided center. Moreover, we show there is a dual pairing between the [MATH]-order universal enveloping algebra of the braided right invariant vector fields and the [MATH]-th jet space of a braided Hopf algebroid and further more a skew pairing between the universal enveloping algebra of its braided right invariant vector fields and its jet Hopf algebroid under a finiteness condition.
tldr: The paper constructs braided Hopf algebroids in braided monoidal categories and studies their associated braided Lie-Rinehart algebras, invariant vector fields, and jet Hopf algebroids.
motivation: The authors aim to generalize Hopf algebroid and Lie-Rinehart algebra theory to the braided (non-symmetric) monoidal setting, with the goal of describing the differential geometry of quantum principal bundles (Hopf Galois extensions).
method: Purely algebraic and categorical techniques: graphical/diagrammatic calculus in braided monoidal categories, Hopf Galois extensions, Ehresmann-Schauenburg Hopf algebroids, universal enveloping algebras, and dual/skew pairings.
result: Right invariant vector fields of braided Ehresmann-Schauenburg Hopf algebroids are shown to be isomorphic to equivariant vector fields on the corresponding quantum principal bundle, and dual/skew pairings are established between enveloping algebras and jet spaces of braided Hopf algebroids.
conclusion: The work provides a unified braided-categorical framework extending Hopf algebroid and Lie algebroid theory, relevant to noncommutative geometry and quantum principal bundles rather than to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Robust Conformal Intrusion Detection Via Traffic-Aware Calibration And Attack-Orbit Invariance
authors: Zhenpeng Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19241v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models fine-tuned for network intrusion detection emit single-point predictions without statistical validity guarantees. Conformal prediction supplies a finite-sample coverage guarantee, but a threshold calibrated on clean traffic fails once an adversary perturbs controllable network features. We demonstrate this failure across three intrusion detection benchmarks and propose traffic-aware conformal prediction, which calibrates on traffic drawn from the perturbation mechanism an attacker is expected to use and provably restores coverage whenever that mechanism is known and can be sampled. A stronger, adaptive attacker that queries the target model's own score can still degrade this matched-calibration guarantee. We address this second threat model by excluding attacker-controllable features and their deterministic descendants from the scored representation, and prove that this yields an exact, pathwise coverage guarantee rather than a probabilistic bound. Across three independently fine-tuned language model architectures, this representation remains completely unchanged under every evaluated attack attempt, at a quantified seven-to-fourteen-point cost in clean accuracy relative to the unrestricted feature set.
tldr: The paper proposes traffic-aware conformal prediction and attacker-invariant feature representations to restore statistical coverage guarantees for LLM-based network intrusion detection under adversarial perturbation.
motivation: Conformal prediction offers finite-sample coverage guarantees for intrusion detection, but a threshold calibrated on clean traffic breaks down once an adversary perturbs controllable network features.
method: The authors calibrate conformal thresholds on traffic drawn from the expected attacker perturbation mechanism, and additionally exclude attacker-controllable features and their deterministic descendants from the scored representation to obtain an exact pathwise coverage guarantee.
result: Matched calibration provably restores coverage when the attack mechanism is known and samplable, while the feature-exclusion approach keeps the representation completely unchanged across all evaluated attacks at a seven-to-fourteen-point cost in clean accuracy.
conclusion: Adversarially robust conformal intrusion detection is achievable via traffic-aware calibration and attack-orbit-invariant representations, at the price of reduced clean-traffic accuracy.

title: Auditplan: Commit, Then Answer For Auditable Safety Alignment
authors: Sai Sri Pushpa Jampani, Kshitij Mishra, Asif Ekbal
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19325v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety tuning pipelines judge only the final answer, which makes it difficult to distinguish robust refusal from two undesirable shortcuts: blanket refusal on benign requests and polished but unfaithful safety rationales that do not actually constrain the answer. We propose AUDITPLAN, a single-model plan-then-answer approach where the model first emits a compact structured safety plan and then answers conditioned on it. The plan records a threat label, intended action, and explicit constraints, enabling machine-checkable auditing while remaining hidden from users at deployment. We train this behavior with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning with FAITHGATE, a reward-gating objective that grants answer reward only when the safety plan is correct. This discourages safe-looking but unfaithful behavior and promotes tighter plan-answer coupling. Across Qwen backbones, AUDITPLAN improves both robustness and auditability: on Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, FAITHGATE reduces ASR from 24.0% to 11.6%, LSR from 1.0% to 0.36%, and over-refusal from 11.0% to 2.0%, outperforming answer-only RL, free-form explanation, and weighted-sum structured rewards. Similar trends hold for Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct. Larger-model confirmation runs on Qwen-3-4B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct preserve the same trend suggesting that explicit internal commitments can make safety alignment more faithful, robust, and auditable.
tldr: AUDITPLAN is a plan-then-answer safety alignment method that uses an auditable internal safety plan and FAITHGATE reward gating to improve robustness and faithfulness in LLM refusal behavior.
motivation: Safety tuning pipelines that judge only final answers cannot distinguish robust refusal from blanket refusal or unfaithful rationales, so a more auditable and faithful safety mechanism is needed.
method: The model first emits a compact structured safety plan (threat label, intended action, constraints), then answers conditioned on it; training combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning using FAITHGATE, which grants answer reward only when the safety plan is correct.
result: On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, FAITHGATE reduces ASR from 24.0% to 11.6%, LSR from 1.0% to 0.36%, and over-refusal from 11.0% to 2.0%, outperforming answer-only RL, free-form explanation, and weighted-sum structured rewards.
conclusion: Explicit internal commitments can make safety alignment more faithful, robust, and auditable, with similar trends on larger Qwen backbones.

title: Scaling Zero Knowledge Unsat Verification Via Normalized Chaining
authors: Ashwin Karthikeyan, Ethan Kharitonov, Kuldeep S. Meel, Anwar Hithnawi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19353v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proofs of UNSAT are a standard primitive in formal verification and software assurance. In many real-world settings, the proof itself encodes proprietary or security-sensitive information, making public disclosure undesirable. Zero-knowledge certification of UNSAT addresses this tension: it enables a prover to convince a verifier that no satisfying assignment exists, without revealing anything about the underlying proof beyond its validity. Luo et al. recently introduced ZkUnsat, a protocol that achieves this goal by proving the validity of a weakened resolution proof in zero knowledge. ZkUnsat demonstrates the feasibility of zero-knowledge certification; however, its scalability to larger, real-world instances is constrained by substantial prover memory overhead, limiting its real-world applicability. Motivated by advances in UNSAT proof formats such as LRAT, which enable efficient plain-text verification, we present a preprocessing technique that improves the efficiency of ZkUnsat without introducing additional leakage. Our approach normalizes the proof so that each derived clause is justified by a resolution chain of fixed public length k. This eliminates chain-length leakage and reduces prover memory usage. With k = 16, our method certifies roughly 62% more instances than baseline ZkUnsat on the SAT 2002 competition benchmarks. Furthermore, for an equivalent number of certified instances, the memory footprint drops to under 25% of that required by the baseline.
tldr: The paper introduces a preprocessing technique for zero-knowledge UNSAT verification that normalizes resolution proofs to fixed-length chains, reducing prover memory and improving scalability.
motivation: Zero-knowledge certification of UNSAT proofs is desirable for formal verification when proofs contain sensitive information, but existing protocols like ZkUnsat suffer from high prover memory overhead that limits real-world scalability.
method: The authors normalize UNSAT proofs so that each derived clause is justified by a resolution chain of fixed public length k, eliminating chain-length leakage and enabling more efficient zero-knowledge verification.
result: With k=16, the method certifies roughly 62% more instances than baseline ZkUnsat on SAT 2002 benchmarks, and for equivalent certified instances, memory footprint drops to under 25% of the baseline.
conclusion: Normalized chaining substantially improves the scalability of zero-knowledge UNSAT certification without additional leakage, making it more practical for larger real-world instances.

title: Almost Optimal Fpt Inapproximability For k-SetCover
authors: Xuandi Ren Venkatesan Guruswami
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that [MATH]-approximate parameterized [MATH]-SetCover is W[1]-hard, and has no [MATH]-time algorithms under ETH. This improves upon the previous best factors [MATH] in (Lin, 2019) and [MATH] in (Karthik, Laekhanukit, and Manurangsi, 2019). Here [MATH] is the yes-case guarantee and [MATH] is the number of candidate sets. While the best approximation ratio is still [MATH] via the greedy algorithm, closing this [MATH] gap in the exponent has been a longstanding open problem; we remove this loss via a simple direct reduction. The construction is self-contained and does not rely on the parameterized inapproximability hypothesis (PIH). Starting with sparse parameterized 2-CSP instances (Karthik, Marx, Pilipczuk, and Souza, 2024), we build a monotone CNF formula, which is equivalent to a SetCover instance. To obtain a [MATH]-versus-[MATH] gap, the reduction enumerates all hash functions from [MATH] to [MATH] and all unsatisfiable 2-CSP instances on the same constraint graph with alphabet [MATH]. For each such instance, it asks for a certificate that the hashed label pairs are not all contained in that instance. Perfect hashing makes this enumeration efficient for [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves nearly optimal parameterized inapproximability for k-SetCover, showing W[1]-hardness and no f(k)·n^{o(k)}-time algorithms under ETH for approximation factors close to the greedy bound.
motivation: Prior work established parameterized inapproximability for k-SetCover but left a gap of a factor of k in the exponent between the best hardness factor and the greedy algorithm's approximation ratio, which had been a longstanding open problem.
method: The reduction starts from sparse parameterized 2-CSP instances and builds a monotone CNF equivalent to a SetCover instance, enumerating all hash functions from a domain to a codomain and all unsatisfiable 2-CSP instances on the same constraint graph, using perfect hashing to keep the enumeration efficient.
result: The authors obtain a direct reduction that removes the loss of a factor of k in the exponent, improving the best previous hardness factors (Lin 2019; Karthik, Laekhanukit, Manurangsi 2019) without relying on the Parameterized Inapproximability Hypothesis (PIH).
conclusion: The work closes a longstanding gap in the exponent of the inapproximability factor for k-SetCover under ETH/W[1]-hardness, providing a simple, self-contained construction.

title: Hopper: Bounded-Memory Collaborative Debiasing For Byzantine-Tolerant Peer Sampling
authors: Joachim Bruneau-Queyreix (labri), Laurent Reveill\`ere (labri), Augusta Mukam
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Byzantine-tolerant peer sampling relies on continuously refreshed views, yet an adversary can bias the identifier streams used to construct them. Frequency-aware debiasing downweights overrepresented identifiers, but existing designs rely on cumulative per-identifier counts. We show that even exact, unbounded counters fail under a delayed balanced attack, in which a long benign prefix masks a subsequent adversarial frequency shift. We introduce Hopper, a bounded-memory debiasing protocol for Byzantine-tolerant peer sampling. We identify the stream-estimation properties required for debiasing and select BitMatcher as the estimator that best preserves adversarial frequency structure among the evaluated alternatives. Hopper adds BMDecay, a saturation-triggered decay and reconstruction mechanism that keeps this signal fresh over long executions. Hopper also supports trusted collaboration through authenticated fingerprint-aware reconstruction and role-specific debiasing. Experiments show that Hopper recovers from delayed attacks faster than when relying on BitMatcher, and debiaising as well as non-debiasing baselines under a fixed memory budget. Trusted collaboration reduces post-attack pollution peaks but creates a re-identification trade-off at high trusted-node densities. These results show the importance of occurence freshness, rather than exact counting alone, as a key requirement for practical frequency-aware Byzantine peer sampling.
tldr: Hopper is a bounded-memory debiasing protocol for Byzantine-tolerant peer sampling that uses BitMatcher and BMDecay to maintain freshness and resist delayed balanced attacks.
motivation: Existing frequency-aware debiasing designs rely on cumulative per-identifier counts and fail under a delayed balanced attack where a long benign prefix masks a subsequent adversarial frequency shift.
method: The authors identify stream-estimation properties required for debiasing, select BitMatcher as the best estimator, and add BMDecay, a saturation-triggered decay and reconstruction mechanism, along with trusted collaboration via authenticated fingerprint-aware reconstruction and role-specific debiasing.
result: Hopper recovers from delayed attacks faster than BitMatcher alone and debiases as well as non-debiasing baselines under a fixed memory budget; trusted collaboration reduces post-attack pollution peaks but creates a re-identification trade-off at high trusted-node densities.
conclusion: Occurrence freshness, rather than exact counting alone, is a key requirement for practical frequency-aware Byzantine peer sampling.

title: Janus: Denial-of-Service Attack Against Beam Hopping In Leo Satellite Networks
authors: Yuval Aviv, Roee Idan, Roy Peled, Asaf Shabtai, Yuval Elovici
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks are increasingly used to provide global connectivity. However, each satellite has limited resources that need to be allocated according to demand, which varies geographically and over time. Beam hopping addresses this challenge by dividing a satellite's service area into geographic cells. Rather than illuminating every cell simultaneously, it dynamically assigns available beams to a selected subset based on demand. This reliance on observed traffic demand as an input to beam-selection decisions creates a new attack surface whose security implications have received little attention. In this paper, we present JANUS, a novel targeted denial-of-service attack against beam-hopping systems in LEO networks. We show that a small botnet of compromised terminals can inject legitimate user traffic into carefully selected non-victim cells to manipulate the beam-hopping scheduler's view of demand. This manipulation alters beam-allocation decisions and redirects service away from the targeted victim area. We evaluate JANUS across different system configurations, schedulers, attack horizons, and attacker-knowledge settings to characterize the attack's effectiveness, required resources, and resulting service disruption over time. Against a rank-based KMAX scheduler, JANUS achieves complete service denial for up to approximately 95% of evaluated victims. Against DRL, JANUS can exclude the victim from approximately 92% of scheduling decisions. Finally, we evaluate mitigation strategies that reduce the attack effectiveness.
tldr: JANUS is a targeted denial-of-service attack that manipulates beam-hopping schedulers in LEO satellite networks by injecting traffic into non-victim cells, redirecting beam allocation away from a victim area.
motivation: Beam hopping in LEO satellite networks relies on observed traffic demand to allocate beams, creating an unexamined attack surface where adversaries can spoof demand to influence scheduling decisions.
method: The authors use a small botnet of compromised terminals to inject legitimate user traffic into carefully selected non-victim cells, then evaluate the resulting service disruption across multiple schedulers, attack horizons, and attacker-knowledge settings, along with candidate mitigations.
result: Against a rank-based KMAX scheduler JANUS achieves near-total service denial for roughly 95% of victims, and against a DRL-based scheduler it excludes the victim from about 92% of scheduling decisions; proposed mitigations reduce but do not eliminate effectiveness.
conclusion: Beam-hopping schedulers are vulnerable to demand-manipulation attacks, and practical defenses are needed to secure resource allocation in LEO satellite networks.

title: Leo Satellite Internet Of Things: Architecture, Technology, And On-Orbit Verification
authors: Ming Ying, Xiaoming Chen, Qiao Qi, Yichao Xu, Jiajun Pan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellations are poised to become a cornerstone of the sixth-generation (6G) Internet of Things (IoT), providing truly global coverage and ubiquitous connectivity. This article presents a holistic two-dimensional system architecture for 6G LEO satellite IoT that incorporates composition and functional perspectives to facilitate the seamless integration of LEO satellites and terrestrial networks. Building upon this architecture, we evaluate three pivotal enabling technologies targeting the uplink, downlink, and inter-satellite links (ISLs). Specifically, we analyze massive grant-free random access for efficient uplink connectivity, investigate deep learning-based multibeam precoding for robust downlink transmission, and examine distributed cooperative routing for resilient ISL data delivery. Furthermore, we present an on-orbit verification platform that validates the real-world feasibility and performance of the proposed solutions. Finally, we outline key open challenges and future research directions to guide the realization of future LEO satellite IoT.
tldr: The paper proposes a two-dimensional system architecture for 6G LEO satellite IoT and evaluates uplink, downlink, and inter-satellite link enabling technologies with an on-orbit verification platform.
motivation: LEO satellite constellations are expected to become a cornerstone of 6G IoT by providing global coverage and ubiquitous connectivity, but seamless integration with terrestrial networks and reliable link performance remain challenging.
method: The authors develop a holistic architecture spanning composition and functional perspectives, and analyze three enabling technologies: massive grant-free random access for uplink, deep learning-based multibeam precoding for downlink, and distributed cooperative routing for inter-satellite links, validated through an on-orbit verification platform.
result: The proposed solutions are validated on an on-orbit platform, demonstrating real-world feasibility and performance for the targeted uplink, downlink, and ISL scenarios, alongside an outline of open challenges.
conclusion: The work provides an architectural and experimental foundation for future LEO satellite IoT in 6G, though it remains an applied classical communications contribution without quantum information, thermodynamics, networking, or hybrid-system content.

title: Voltage-Current-Emission Framework Of Time-Resolved Electroluminescence
authors: Hui Bao, Longjia Wu, Yanan Guo, Jianchang Yan, Ying Wang, Haizheng Zhong
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19723v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-resolved electroluminescence has been a central methodology in the development of LED devices. However, it still lacks quantitative theoretical descriptions of time-resolved electroluminescence. By combining the equivalent circuit models of semiconductor devices and the carrier dynamics of electroluminescence processes, we here developed a Voltage-Current-Emission framework to illustrate time-resolved electroluminescence from the pulse voltage as input, to injection current and finally generate electroluminescence as output. The features of different LED devices can be quantitatively interpreted, confirming the universal applicability across LEDs with different materials and device structures. Importantly, the curves of time-resolved electroluminescence can be simulated to quantitatively describe the dynamics of current and carriers of LED operation. In all, the Voltage-Current-Emission framework offers theoretical guidance for achieving advanced LED devices for AI technology.
tldr: The paper proposes a voltage-current-emission framework that combines equivalent circuit models with carrier dynamics to quantitatively describe time-resolved electroluminescence in LEDs.
motivation: Time-resolved electroluminescence is widely used in LED development, but lacks quantitative theoretical descriptions linking voltage pulses, current, and emission dynamics.
method: The authors integrate equivalent circuit models of semiconductor devices with carrier dynamics to derive a voltage-current-emission framework, which they use to simulate time-resolved electroluminescence curves for various LED devices.
result: The framework quantitatively reproduces experimental time-resolved electroluminescence features across LEDs with different materials and structures, enabling extraction of current and carrier dynamics.
conclusion: This voltage-current-emission framework provides theoretical guidance for advanced LED device design, particularly for AI-related technologies, but does not address quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Hausdorff Spectrum Of Lyapunov Exponents For Higher-dimensional Self-affine Systems
authors: Reza Mohammadpour Bal\'azs B\'ar\'any
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19309v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the Hausdorff dimension of projections of level sets of Lyapunov exponents for affine iterated function systems. Assuming that the tuple of linear parts is typical, we obtain a variational formula in terms of pressure, topological entropy, and the Lyapunov dimensions of invariant measures corresponding to Lyapunov exponents. In [MATH], we show that this value equals the Hausdorff dimension of the canonical projection of the level set under the strong open set condition. We further extend the result to arbitrary dimensions, showing that the same formula holds for Lebesgue-almost every choice of translation vectors under a suitable contraction assumption.
tldr: The paper studies the Hausdorff dimension of level sets of Lyapunov exponents for affine iterated function systems, deriving a variational formula under typical linear parts and extending it to all dimensions under a contraction assumption.
motivation: Understanding the fine-scale geometry of Lyapunov exponent level sets is a central problem in the dimension theory of self-affine dynamical systems.
method: The authors use pressure, topological entropy, and Lyapunov dimensions of invariant measures to formulate a variational principle, and apply the strong open set condition to relate the formula to the Hausdorff dimension of canonical projections.
result: For typical linear parts, the Hausdorff dimension of projections of Lyapunov exponent level sets equals a variational expression, and the same formula holds for Lebesgue-almost every translation vector in arbitrary dimensions under a suitable contraction assumption.
conclusion: This establishes a dimension formula for Lyapunov exponent spectra in higher-dimensional self-affine systems, contributing to fractal geometry and dynamical systems theory.

title: Optimal Strategies In A Sequential Contest With Failures
authors: Alec Pannunzio, Ashley Shaffer, Gregory Shaver, Shreyas Sundaram
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19706v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a Stackelberg model where two players compete in a sequential contest, and the player that successfully invests the most effort wins. Our formulation considers a probability that each player fails to invest their chosen level of effort, as captured by a failure function that increases with the amount of effort. The players each have their own cost of failure, as well as a maximum level of effort (capturing different abilities of the players). We prove three key results. First, we provide the optimal strategy for Player 1 (the follower), to maximize their utility given an observed effort exerted by Player 2 (the leader). Next, we characterize the optimal strategy to maximize the expected utility of Player 2, anticipating the optimal response by Player 1. Finally, we analyze the expected utilities of each player when both play their optimal strategy, and provide key insights into how heterogeneous player abilities and failure costs affect the outcomes of the game.
tldr: The paper analyzes optimal strategies in a sequential two-player contest where effort investment can fail with a probability that increases with effort.
motivation: The authors aim to understand how heterogeneous abilities, failure probabilities, and failure costs affect strategic behavior in a Stackelberg contest.
method: They model the game with a failure function, derive the follower's best response to observed leader effort, then characterize the leader's optimal strategy anticipating that response.
result: They provide closed-form optimal strategies for both players and analyze expected utilities, showing how player abilities and failure costs influence outcomes.
conclusion: The work offers insights into sequential contests with probabilistic failures, but it is a game-theoretic study unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Strategic Pricing In Electricity Markets With Pollution Constraints
authors: Luce Brotcorne (INOCS), Ga\"el Guillot (INOCS), Alejandro Jofr\'e (CMM), Benjam\'in Vera
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a new model for a regulated day-ahead type auction-based electrical market in which the system operator can measure and limit the producer's emissions when choosing its optimal dispatch. We prove properties of this market model that describe it as a generalization to other previous works in the electrical market literature. Furthermore, we use standard sensitivity analysis tools to measure the impact of these pollution variables on market equilibria and present numerical examples of this effect.
tldr: Introduces a regulated day-ahead electricity auction model in which the system operator can measure and limit producers' emissions while choosing optimal dispatch.
motivation: To incorporate pollution constraints into electricity market clearing and analyze their impact on market equilibria.
method: Formulates an auction-based market model with emission limits, proves structural properties, and applies sensitivity analysis with numerical examples.
result: Shows the model generalizes prior electricity market formulations and quantifies how pollution variables affect equilibria.
conclusion: The framework can support the design and regulation of electricity markets subject to environmental constraints.

title: Alibi: Adversarial Legitimacy Injection In Binary Input Against Llm Malware Analyzers
authors: Hyeongjun Choi, Wonyoung Jung, Haehoon Seo, Sungyup Nam
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19722v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are being integrated into malware triage workflows as reasoning components that summarize static evidence and produce analyst-facing verdicts. This paper shows that the same reasoning capability introduces a new attack surface. We present ALIBI, a semantic cover story attack against frontier LLM-based malware analyzers. ALIBI adds a small, non-executed read-only section to a compiled binary, containing a coherent but false security product narrative, without altering imports or executable behavior. Instead of issuing direct instructions to the model, it reframes suspicious evidence as expected behavior of a benign endpoint security tool. On a frozen PE set of 50 malicious samples, the payload flips 30 of the 35 baseline-malicious samples to benign on Gemini 2.5 Pro, while GPT-5.5 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7 produce substantial severity downgrades with significant confidence reductions even when verdict labels are preserved. The attack transfers to ELF binaries, where Gemini flips 16 of 40. A verification-guided defense prompt roughly halves the benign verdicts, but 42.9 percent of malicious samples still reach benign. LLM malware analyzers therefore require provenance checks that separate verified facts from attacker-controlled claims, not narrative trust.
tldr: The paper introduces ALIBI, a semantic cover story attack that injects benign security-product narratives into binary files to manipulate LLM-based malware analyzers into downgrading malicious verdicts.
motivation: As LLMs are increasingly used in malware triage, their reasoning capability may create new attack surfaces that adversaries can exploit to mislead analysts.
method: ALIBI adds a small, non-executed read-only section containing a coherent false narrative to compiled PE and ELF binaries, reframing suspicious evidence as expected behavior of a benign endpoint security tool without changing executable behavior.
result: On a frozen PE set of 50 malicious samples, the attack flipped 30 of 35 baseline-malicious samples to benign on Gemini 2.5 Pro, and caused substantial severity downgrades on GPT-5.5 Pro and Claude Opus 4.7; it also transferred to ELF binaries and partially resisted a verification-guided defense prompt.
conclusion: LLM malware analyzers must implement provenance checks that separate verified facts from attacker-controlled claims rather than trusting narrative context.

title: Existence And Non-existence In Common Hypercyclicity And Its Frequent Variants
authors: Romuald Ernst (LMPA), Fernando Vieira Costa Junior (UFPB), Monia Mestiri (LML), Augustin Mouze
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19219v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a family [MATH] of bounded linear operators acting on the same [MATH]-space [MATH] and indexed by a set of parameters [MATH], [MATH], we explore the existence and non-existence of vectors that simultaneously satisfy, for all elements of [MATH], one of the following three dynamical properties: hypercyclicity, upper frequent hypercyclicity, and frequent hypercyclicity. Our approach relies on associating to [MATH] a "Lipschitz constant function'' [MATH], whose growth encodes the interaction between the operators and the parameter set [MATH]. We show that the asymptotic behavior of [MATH] determines sharp thresholds between existence and non-existence of common vectors. In the hypercyclicity setting, we identify the divergence of [MATH], where [MATH] is the Hausdorff dimension of [MATH], as a natural condition for existence, and prove complementary non-existence results, which are optimal for weighted shifts. For upper frequent hypercyclicity, we obtain criteria of non-existence in terms of series of the form [MATH] for parameter sets in [MATH]-dimensions. Considered in the one-dimensional case, these criteria are optimal and allow us to contrast known existence results of Mestiri for logarithmic-type growth with non-existence beyond this scale. For frequent hypercyclicity, we establish a dichotomy showing that common vectors exist essentially only when [MATH] is bounded, while any unbounded growth prevents their existence. Our results apply to a broad class of parameter sets, including self-similar fractals, providing a unified perspective on how growth conditions and geometric features of [MATH] determine common dynamical behavior. Finally, in the specific context of weighted shifts, we prove that two operators do not necessarily share the same frequently hypercyclic vectors if the sequence of their weight products ratios admits two distinct non-zero cluster points, establishing the optimality of a result of Grivaux, Matheron and Menet.
tldr: A pure mathematics paper characterizing existence and non-existence of common hypercyclic, upper frequently hypercyclic, and frequently hypercyclic vectors for parameterized families of bounded linear operators.
motivation: The authors aim to unify and sharpen criteria for when families of operators share vectors exhibiting various dynamical (hypercyclic) properties, linking these to geometric features of the parameter set.
method: They introduce a 'Lipschitz constant function' whose asymptotic growth encodes operator-parameter interaction, and derive sharp thresholds via Hausdorff dimension and series criteria, with optimality results for weighted shifts.
result: They obtain existence/non-existence thresholds governed by the divergence of the Lipschitz function, a dichotomy for frequent hypercyclicity (common vectors exist essentially only when the function is bounded), and sharp weighted-shift optimality results.
conclusion: The work provides a unified framework showing how growth conditions and fractal geometry of parameter sets determine common dynamical behavior, resolving optimality of prior results.

title: Sobolev Mixing Constants And Compactness In Rational Moduli Space
authors: Ilya Krishtal Alastair Fletcher
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study uniformity of Sobolev mixing estimates for rational maps and uniformly quasiregular mappings. For rational maps of fixed degree, the optimal centered Sobolev trace constant [MATH] is a continuous proper function on M\"obius moduli space. Uniform bounds on [MATH] therefore characterize relative compactness in moduli, and a minimizing class exists in every degree. In the setting of uniformly quasiregular endomorphisms of degree [MATH] on closed [MATH]-manifolds with an invariant conformal structure, the [MATH]th centered transfer operator from critical Sobolev energy into [MATH] of the equilibrium measure has norm [MATH]. On the mean-zero Sobolev space, the spectrum and Fredholm essential spectrum are the closed disk of radius [MATH], with infinite-dimensional eigenspaces throughout its interior. The proofs use the energy scaling of pullback, a bounded equilibrium trace, and an obstruction from atoms of intermediate mass. Combined with conformal barycenter normalization and DeMarco--Faber's degeneration theorem, this obstruction gives the moduli compactness criterion. Explicit families illustrate the distinction between degeneration and concentration caused by changes of coordinates.
tldr: The paper studies Sobolev mixing constants for rational maps and uniformly quasiregular mappings, linking uniform bounds to compactness in moduli space and analyzing transfer operator spectra.
motivation: The authors aim to understand uniformity and compactness phenomena in rational moduli space through Sobolev trace constants and transfer operators.
method: They use energy scaling of pullback, bounded equilibrium trace, an obstruction from atoms of intermediate mass, conformal barycenter normalization, and DeMarco--Faber's degeneration theorem.
result: The optimal centered Sobolev trace constant is a continuous proper function on Möbius moduli space, uniform bounds characterize relative compactness, and the transfer operator has norm one with spectrum the closed unit disk and infinite-dimensional eigenspaces.
conclusion: The work provides a moduli compactness criterion and illustrates degeneration versus concentration caused by coordinate changes.

title: Human-Anchored Inference For Ranking New Models With Large Language Model Judges
authors: Xin Zhou, Sinian Zhang, Zhanyan Yang, Mingyuan Xu, Molei Liu, Doudou Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19599v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human pairwise comparisons provide a reference for evaluating large language models (LLMs), but collecting sufficient judgments for each new release is costly and time-consuming. LLM judges offer a scalable alternative, although their comparisons may differ systematically from human preferences and across judges. We study the ranking of a new model that has received LLM-judge comparisons but no human comparisons. We propose ANCHOR (ANchored Comparisons for Human-reference inference with Orthogonal Riesz correction), which uses historical human and LLM comparisons to learn judge-specific sensitivities to human score differences and feature-dependent judge biases. These estimates are then used to infer the new model's human-reference score from its judge comparisons. The framework allows the feature distribution to change between historical and new-model comparisons. For inference, we construct a Neyman-orthogonal estimator through a joint Riesz correction that removes the first-order effects of estimating the historical human scores, judge sensitivities, and bias functions. We establish identification, convergence rates, and asymptotic normality with consistently estimable variance, and show that ANCHOR attains the semiparametric efficiency bound. Simulations demonstrate gains in score estimation and ranking accuracy. On Chatbot Arena, ANCHOR achieves the lowest score RMSE and insertion MAE among competing methods, with narrower score intervals on average.
tldr: ANCHOR is a statistical inference framework that uses historical human and LLM-judge comparisons to infer a new LLM's human-reference quality score when only judge comparisons are available.
motivation: Evaluating newly released LLMs against human preferences requires costly human pairwise comparisons, while LLM judges are scalable but systematically biased and inconsistent across judges.
method: The authors model judge-specific sensitivities to human score differences and feature-dependent judge biases, then construct a Neyman-orthogonal estimator via a joint Riesz correction to remove first-order effects of nuisance estimation.
result: The estimator is shown to be semiparametrically efficient with established identification, convergence rates, and asymptotic normality; simulations and Chatbot Arena experiments show the lowest score RMSE and insertion MAE among competitors.
conclusion: The approach enables reliable human-referenced ranking of new models from judge comparisons alone, even under distribution shift in features.

title: Online Material-Labeled Environment Reconstruction Via Bayesian Multipath Attribution For Low-Altitude Isac
authors: Meihui Liu, Shu Sun, Ruifeng Gao, Qiuming Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19819v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Environment reconstruction for low-altitude integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) has largely focused on geometry-centric maps, overlooking material-dependent propagation effects. Material-labeled reconstruction is therefore a key step toward propagation-aware mapping, enabling more physically grounded channel prediction and uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) networking. However, constructing such maps from wireless multipath observations is challenging in outdoor multi-building scenarios because multipath components (MPCs) from different facades are mixed, path-to-facade attribution is uncertain, and UAV measurements arrive sequentially under time-varying observation geometries. To address these challenges, we propose a unified online probabilistic framework that represents each reflecting facade as a virtual anchor (VA) and couples Bayesian VA localization, multipath attribution, and material inference. The Bayesian front end estimates facade-level geometry and computes soft MPC-to-VA attribution probabilities using a speculardiffuse likelihood model, thereby accounting for both dominant specular paths and diffuse surface-interacted components. These attribution probabilities are used to construct attribution-aware MPC representations, which are aggregated in a VA-centric manner and mapped by a material inference network to facadelevel material evidence. The resulting evidence is recursively fused through an online Bayesian update to produce stable material posteriors and material-labeled environment maps. Ray-tracing simulations in a representative urban street scenario show that the proposed method substantially outperforms a no-attribution baseline, achieves 93.75% final facade-level material accuracy on a held-out UAV trajectory, and maintains accurate VA-based facade localization.
tldr: The paper proposes an online Bayesian framework for material-labeled environment reconstruction in low-altitude ISAC by coupling virtual-anchor localization, multipath attribution, and material inference.
motivation: Environment reconstruction for low-altitude ISAC has focused on geometry-centric maps while ignoring material-dependent propagation effects that matter for physically grounded channel prediction and UAV networking.
method: Each reflecting facade is modeled as a virtual anchor, with a Bayesian front end computing soft MPC-to-VA attribution probabilities via a specular-diffuse likelihood model; these attribution-aware representations feed a material inference network whose evidence is recursively fused online.
result: Ray-tracing simulations in an urban street scenario show substantial improvement over a no-attribution baseline, 93.75% final facade-level material accuracy on a held-out UAV trajectory, and accurate VA-based facade localization.
conclusion: The unified online probabilistic framework enables stable material posteriors and material-labeled environment maps from sequential wireless multipath observations, advancing propagation-aware mapping for ISAC and UAV networks.

title: Entropy-Based Local Characteristic Decomposition
authors: Shaoshuai Chu, Michael Herty, Alexander Kurganov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19838v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local characteristic decomposition (LCD) is widely used in high-order numerical methods for hyperbolic systems of conservation laws to reduce spurious oscillations appearing in the computed solutions. The LCD implementation requires a representative average interface state, typically obtained using arithmetic or Roe-type averages of the nearly grid values. We propose an entropy-based LCD (ELCD), in which the states in the two cells adjacent to an interface are considered together with several nearby states in phase space. Among these candidates, we select the state that locally minimizes the entropy and use it as an average interface state for linearizing the flux Jacobian. We incorporate the ELCD into several second-order finite-volume and fifth-order finite-difference schemes. Numerical experiments for the two-dimensional Euler equations of gas dynamics show that the schemes, which utilize the ELCD procedure generally resolve complex wave structures more sharply than their counterparts, which use the arithmetic averages.
tldr: The paper introduces an entropy-based local characteristic decomposition (ELCD) that selects an interface state minimizing entropy among neighboring candidates, improving the sharpness of high-order finite-volume and finite-difference schemes for hyperbolic conservation laws.
motivation: Local characteristic decomposition is used in high-order numerical schemes to suppress spurious oscillations, but it relies on arbitrary arithmetic or Roe-type averages of adjacent grid values as the interface state.
method: The authors consider the two cell-adjacent states together with nearby phase-space candidates and pick the one locally minimizing entropy as the representative average interface state for linearizing the flux Jacobian, embedding this into second-order finite-volume and fifth-order finite-difference schemes.
result: Numerical experiments on the two-dimensional Euler equations of gas dynamics show that schemes using ELCD resolve complex wave structures more sharply than those using arithmetic averages.
conclusion: Entropy-based selection of interface states provides a practical improvement for high-order shock-capturing schemes in computational gas dynamics.

title: Determination Of The Output Injection Of Invertible Linear Systems For Guaranteeing A Regular Relative Degree
authors: Shida Cao, Bin Zhou, Guang-Ren Duan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For an invertible linear time-invariant system, the Morse normal form reveals that there exist an output injection and an output transformation such that the resulting system possesses a regular relative degree. Based on this fact, this paper develops a method to determine all admissible output injections and output transformations that achieve this property. In contrast to the recursive and implicit computation methods in the existing literature, the proposed determination method for the output injections is explicit and easy to use, since the solutions are obtained by solving linear matrix equations. A rigorous proof of the proposed method is provided, and an illustrative example is presented to demonstrate the applicability of the approach.
tldr: The paper develops an explicit method to determine all output injections and output transformations that give an invertible linear time-invariant system a regular relative degree.
motivation: The Morse normal form guarantees the existence of output injections and transformations yielding a regular relative degree, but existing recursive implicit methods are cumbersome and hard to use.
method: The authors solve linear matrix equations to characterize all admissible output injections and output transformations, providing a rigorous proof and an illustrative example.
result: The proposed determination method is explicit, easy to use, and avoids the recursive implicit computation found in prior literature.
conclusion: This work simplifies the computation of output injections for regular relative degree assignment in linear systems, with potential applications in control theory.

title: Papc: Platform Mediation For Privacy-Propagation Externalities In AI-Mediated Workflows
authors: Tao Huang, Guosen Wu, Chen Hou, Guolong Zheng
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-mediated platforms coordinate work through LLM agents acting for different principals. In these workflows, privacy loss can be created before a final answer appears: a memory write, shared-workspace update, inter-agent message, or tool event may impose downstream exposure cost on another principal. We model this failure mode as a privacy-propagation externality, where the cost of a raw disclosure depends on topology and fanout as well as content. We present PAPC, a platform-mediated mechanism that intercepts information-moving events before they update shared state or external channels. PAPC combines policy, provenance, topology/fanout, privilege, and content signals to allow an event, release a policy-safe abstraction, quarantine raw content, block a transition, or narrow onward rights. The model explains why final-output control misses intermediate exposure costs and why high-fanout objects amplify propagation. Across retrieval-memory and multi-agent workflow benchmarks, PAPC preserves deterministic task completion and eliminates measured exact raw-value and external raw-value exposure. The results position event-level mediation as a platform-governance primitive for agent-mediated online work.
tldr: PAPC is a platform-mediated mechanism that intercepts information-moving events in LLM-agent workflows to prevent privacy-propagation externalities from intermediate disclosures.
motivation: In AI-mediated platforms, privacy loss can occur before a final answer appears—through memory writes, shared-workspace updates, inter-agent messages, or tool events—imposing downstream exposure costs that final-output controls fail to capture.
method: The authors model this as a privacy-propagation externality whose cost depends on topology and fanout, and implement PAPC, an event-level mediation mechanism combining policy, provenance, topology/fanout, privilege, and content signals to allow, abstract, quarantine, block, or narrow rights.
result: Across retrieval-memory and multi-agent workflow benchmarks, PAPC preserves deterministic task completion while eliminating measured exact raw-value and external raw-value exposure.
conclusion: Event-level mediation is positioned as a platform-governance primitive for agent-mediated online work, addressing intermediate exposure costs that output-level controls miss.

title: Efficient Nash Equilibrium Computation For Cybersecurity Games
authors: Michael Lanier, David Farmer, Yevgeniy Vorobeychik
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Computing Nash equilibria of simulation-based cybersecurity games with policy-space response oracles (PSRO) is bottlenecked by payoff estimation: every payoff-matrix entry costs Monte-Carlo rollouts of a slow simulator, while policies and restricted-game solves are cheap. We introduce Regret-Weighted Payoff Sampling (RWPS), a budgeted estimator that simulates only the cells an equilibrium is sensitive to and fills the rest with a surrogate trained on every entry simulated earlier in the run. The sup-norm error bound cannot evaluate such an estimator, because it is set by the cells left deliberately inaccurate. We prove an instance-dependent bound that weights error by the opponent's equilibrium mixture, a certificate computable from simulation data alone, and a coverage result showing that once the deviation-relevant set is simulated, surrogate error cannot affect either player's regret. On three 21x21 general-sum games, two synthetic and an asymmetric Colonel Blotto, the refined bounds are four to six times tighter on the estimator's own output, and the coverage result predicts in advance which games are cheap: 18% of the matrix for small-support games against 82% for Blotto. In growing-pool PSRO, RWPS reaches lower exploitability than minimum-regret-first search, information-gain search, and progressive sampling at a matched budget, and on the CyGym and ANSG cyber simulators it is lowest at the smallest budgets.
tldr: RWPS is a budgeted payoff-sampling estimator with instance-dependent error bounds that speeds up Nash equilibrium computation in simulation-based cybersecurity games.
motivation: Computing Nash equilibria in simulation-based security games via PSRO is bottlenecked by expensive Monte-Carlo payoff estimation, since each payoff-matrix entry requires slow simulator rollouts.
method: The authors introduce Regret-Weighted Payoff Sampling, which simulates only the equilibrium-sensitive cells and fills the rest with a surrogate model, and prove an instance-dependent error bound weighted by the opponent's equilibrium mixture.
result: On three 21x21 general-sum games the refined bounds are 4-6x tighter, coverage predictions distinguish cheap (18%) from expensive (82%) games, and RWPS achieves lower exploitability at matched budgets on CyGym and ANSG simulators.
conclusion: RWPS offers a principled, certificate-based approach to efficient equilibrium computation in large simulation-based security games, though it lies entirely outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Trust, But Validate The Instrument: Auditing AI-Generated Rtl Verification Plans On Authored Security-Regression Proxies
authors: Hang Xiao, Chuhong Xu, Kainan Zhou, Gangzhen Qian, Lu Yi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-generated RTL verification plans can satisfy a provider schema yet fail at the boundary to trusted execution. We present SecTB-RTL, an auditable framework covering 31 tasks and 124 authored hardware-security regressions. A deterministic non-AI baseline killed 36, 75, and 78 mutants at increasing resource limits. The first confirmatory run (C1-R2) failed before model execution because the provider rejected its response schema. After a schema-only repair made without viewing outcomes, a separately frozen follow-up run (C1-R3) completed 1,860 calls. The provider accepted 1,857 responses, but only nine passed the production semantic validator. The generation and execution rules did not match. We therefore preserve the run as an instrument-validation incident and report no prompt-effect estimate. This incident shows that provider or schema acceptance does not establish execution validity. Compilation and coverage are only diagnostics; the exact saved artifact must pass the full production path. A subsequent follow-up is excluded because it did not satisfy the preregistered evidence-completeness gate and is treated only as future work. We release the benchmark, failure-preserving contract, incident provenance, and governance controls needed to prevent infrastructure behavior from being misreported as model behavior.
tldr: SecTB-RTL is an auditable framework for evaluating AI-generated RTL verification plans, which documents a provider/schema-acceptance failure rather than a model-effect result.
motivation: AI-generated hardware verification plans can satisfy a provider's response schema while still failing semantic validation at the trusted-execution boundary, so infrastructure acceptance must not be conflated with execution validity.
method: The authors build a benchmark of 31 tasks and 124 authored hardware-security regressions, compare against a deterministic non-AI mutant-killing baseline, and run frozen confirmatory experiments (C1-R2, C1-R3) with a production semantic validator and a preregistered evidence-completeness gate.
result: The baseline killed 36, 75, and 78 mutants; in C1-R3 the provider accepted 1,857 of 1,860 responses but only nine passed the production semantic validator, revealing a mismatch between generation and execution rules.
conclusion: The run is preserved as an instrument-validation incident with no prompt-effect estimate, and the authors release the benchmark, failure-preserving contract, provenance, and governance controls to prevent infrastructure behavior from being misreported as model behavior.

title: ResumeShield: Channel Separation And An Open Benchmark For Indirect Prompt Injection In Ai Resume Screening
authors: Jay Barach
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An AI resume screener reads a document supplied by the person it is evaluating, inverting the usual trust relationship between an assessor and the material it assesses. Candidates exploit this by concealing instructions inside a resume using white text, zero font size, hidden elements, markup comments, document metadata, or zero width characters. A human reviewer sees nothing, while a naive extraction pipeline places the concealed text into the model prompt, where it is read as an instruction and obeyed. This is indirect prompt injection, listed as LLM01:2025 by OWASP, and recent measurement work reports it in roughly one percent of resumes in a production screening corpus. We present ResumeShield, an open-source defense and benchmark. The defense combines three filtering stages with a fourth architectural stage that places candidate content in an explicitly fenced data channel that the operator's trusted instructions declare inert. The benchmark builds a seeded synthetic corpus spanning nine concealment techniques and two payload families, one using documented phrasings and one modeling an adaptive attacker who paraphrases around the filter, and it scores an attack as successful only when the screening outcome changes. On a corpus of 104 documents, the naive pipeline is manipulated in every injected case while the defended pipeline is never manipulated. Detection reaches a precision of 1.000 and a recall of 0.944 with no false positives on clean resumes. An ablation shows that channel separation alone removes all measured attack success, whereas the complete filtering stack without separation still leaves 16.7 percent of attacks effective. We also identify a concealment dilemma: every payload that evaded detection was one the attacker left visible, surrendering the invisibility that motivates the attack. ResumeShield is released under the Apache 2.0 license with synthetic data only.
tldr: ResumeShield is an open-source defense and benchmark against indirect prompt injection attacks hidden in AI-screened resumes, using multi-stage filtering plus an architectural channel-separation design.
motivation: AI resume screeners consume documents supplied by the very candidates being evaluated, inverting the usual trust relationship and enabling hidden-instruction attacks (OWASP LLM01).
method: The authors combine three content-filtering stages with a fourth architectural stage that places candidate text in an explicitly fenced data channel declared inert by the operator's trusted instructions, evaluated on a seeded synthetic corpus of 104 documents spanning nine concealment techniques and two payload families.
result: The naive pipeline was manipulated in every injected case, while the defended pipeline was never manipulated, achieving precision 1.000 and recall 0.944 with no false positives; ablation shows channel separation alone eliminates attack success while filtering alone leaves 16.7% effective.
conclusion: Channel separation is the decisive defense, and a 'concealment dilemma' means surviving payloads must be visible, undermining the attack's purpose; the benchmark is released under Apache 2.0 with synthetic data only.

title: Site-scale, Multi-resolution Wrf Wind Modeling With Observational Nudging For Methane Emission Monitoring In The Permian Basin
authors: Ehsan Kharazmi, Erin Menezes, George Karniadakis, Anantha Sundaram, Arash Fathi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19442v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate methane source localization and emission-rate estimation at oil and gas facilities require wind fields that resolve site-scale spatial and temporal variability, which cannot be characterized by a single anemometer or coarse operational weather products. We develop a multiscale Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) framework for a Permian Basin facility that dynamically downscales hourly, 3 km High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) fields through four nested domains with grid spacings of 3 km, 1 km, 200 m, and 40 m. The two outer domains use planetary-boundary-layer parameterization, whereas the two inner domains operate in large-eddy-simulation mode. One-minute wind observations from two on-site anemometers are assimilated through wind-only observational nudging in the innermost domain, and the effects of nesting feedback and turbulence-closure choices are examined. Simulations for winter and summer 2025 periods are evaluated using near-surface wind-speed time series, power spectra, spatial fields, and statistical metrics. The baseline simulation reproduces the broad evolution of observed wind events but drifts during weak-wind periods. Observational nudging with one- and two-way nesting reduces the absolute bias of wind-speed by %65 at one sensor and %87 at the other, while reducing the corresponding root-mean-square errors by %33 and %44. Nudging also increases high-frequency energy and resolved spatial gradients, although improvements in turbulence statistics are not uniform. These results demonstrate a practical physics-based pathway for generating high-resolution wind fields for methane-plume modeling while emphasizing the need for independent spatial observations to validate accuracy away from assimilated sensors.
tldr: This paper develops a multiscale WRF modeling framework with observational nudging to generate high-resolution wind fields for methane emission monitoring in the Permian Basin.
motivation: Accurate methane source localization and emission-rate estimation require wind fields that resolve site-scale spatial and temporal variability, which coarse weather products and single anemometers cannot provide.
method: The authors dynamically downscale hourly 3 km HRRR fields through four nested WRF domains (3 km, 1 km, 200 m, 40 m), using PBL parameterization in outer domains and LES mode in inner domains, and assimilate one-minute wind observations from two on-site anemometers via wind-only observational nudging.
result: Observational nudging with one- and two-way nesting reduces absolute wind-speed bias by 65% and 87% at the two sensors, and reduces RMSE by 33% and 44%, while increasing high-frequency energy and spatial gradients but not uniformly improving turbulence statistics.
conclusion: The study demonstrates a practical physics-based pathway for generating high-resolution wind fields for methane-plume modeling, while highlighting the need for independent spatial observations to validate accuracy away from assimilated sensors.

title: Sparse Pointwise Bounds For Maximal Truncations Of Rough Singular Integrals And Sobolev-type Inequalities
authors: Diego Chamorro (lamme), Anca-Nicoleta Marcoci, Liviu-Gabriel Marcoci
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19185v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] and let Omega be in [MATH] with vanishing mean. We prove that the maximal truncation [MATH] of the rough singular integral [MATH] is pointwise dominated by finitely many sparse potentials of the form: [MATH], where [MATH] and [MATH]. This estimate is uniform in the truncation parameter and extends the subcritical bound of Hoang, Moen, and Perez for [MATH] to [MATH]. Since the argument does not require the boundedness of [MATH] on the target space, it yields two-weight Sobolev inequalities: [MATH], under joint two-weight conditions, while the target weight u itself is only required to belong to [MATH]. Additionally, we prove a Hedberg-type estimate involving a Morrey norm of the gradient and apply it to weighted grand Lebesgue spaces. Further consequences are obtained in weighted Lebesgue, Orlicz, and variable Lebesgue spaces.
tldr: The paper proves sparse pointwise bounds for maximal truncations of rough singular integrals and derives Sobolev-type inequalities in weighted function spaces.
motivation: The authors aim to extend subcritical sparse domination results for rough singular integrals to the full range and obtain two-weight Sobolev inequalities without assuming boundedness on the target space.
method: They show that the maximal truncation operator is pointwise dominated by finitely many sparse potentials, uniformly in the truncation parameter, and use this to establish two-weight Sobolev inequalities under joint weight conditions.
result: They obtain pointwise sparse bounds for rough singular integrals, two-weight Sobolev inequalities with target weight in a certain class, a Hedberg-type estimate involving Morrey norms, and applications to weighted grand Lebesgue, Orlicz, and variable Lebesgue spaces.
conclusion: The results extend known sparse domination and Sobolev-type inequalities to broader settings, with further consequences in several weighted function spaces.

title: A Consistent Failure Of Separable Quotients For Pointwise Function Spaces
authors: Jerzy K\k{a}kol Tomasz Kania
abstract: ArXiv:2609.19351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Assuming Jensen's diamond principle, we construct an infinite compact zero-dimensional space [MATH] such that [MATH] has no infinite-dimensional Hausdorff separable linear quotient. The space [MATH] is separable and crowded, has weight [MATH] and cardinality [MATH], and is an Efimov space. We construct [MATH] as an inverse limit of compact metrisable spaces indexed by the countable ordinals.
